docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Step-by-Step Introduction to the [NestJS] Web Framework

Created by the Claude AI from Anthropic at the request of Serge Tahé - September 2026

This document is a translation of the original French version, generated using an automated tool. Some expressions or technical terms may not fully reflect the original meaning.

This course shows, step by step, how to build an MVC web application with the NestJS framework and the TypeScript language. The HTML pages are generated by the server with the Handlebars view engine, with no JavaScript framework in the browser.

It starts with 28 small projects, each focused on a single concept: controllers, actions and routing; modules and dependency injection; converting and validating parameters with pipes; Handlebars views, layouts, partials and helpers; forms, validation and the Post / Redirect / Get pattern; internationalization; data scopes; the request life cycle (middleware, guards, interceptors, pipes, exception filters); JWT authentication in a cookie, roles, captcha and rate limiting; and finally a layered web / business / DAO architecture with TypeORM and MySQL, with transactions and optimistic locking.

Then comes a complete case study, RdvMedecins: an appointment-booking application for a medical practice, made of about sixty files that are all commented, with three roles (administrator, doctors, patients) and a French and English interface built with Bootstrap 5.

Prerequisites: the basics of web programming (HTTP, HTML). The course follows the progression of the course Introduction to the ASP.NET MVC Framework through Examples (2013), adapted to Node.js and TypeScript.

This course is the first in a series that covers the same 28 examples, number by number, with other frameworks: ASP.NET Core MVC, Spring MVC, Flask, Laravel, Symfony and Django.

All courses by Serge Tahé

docs.title: 13.1. Installation of Node.js
docs.text:
[Node.js] is downloaded to nodejs.org: select version LTS (long-term support), 20 or higher. The [Windows] installer also installs [npm]. Verify the installation in a console ([PowerShell] or command prompt):

node --version
npm --version

The examples do not require installing the [nest] tool globally: it is included as a dependency in the [examples] folder and the case study, and can be accessed via [npx nest].

docs.title: 13.2. Installing Visual Studio Code
docs.text: [Visual Studio Code] is downloaded from code.visualstudio.com. It includes [TypeScript] without an extension. For views, the Handlebars extension (syntax highlighting for [.hbs] files) is useful. Open the [examples] folder (File menu / Open Folder); the built-in terminal (Terminal menu / New Terminal) allows you to run the [npm] and [npx] commands without leaving the editor.

docs.title: 13.3. Installing MySQL with Laragon
docs.text:
[Laragon] (laragon.org) installs a [MySQL] server (or [MariaDB]) ready for use, along with the [HeidiSQL] administration tool. After installation:

  • the "Start All" button launches the [MySQL] server on port 3306;
  • the user [root] has no password: these are the default values from Example 28;
  • the "Database" button opens [HeidiSQL], where the File / Run File SQL runs the scripts [dbpersons.sql] (Example 28) and [dbrdvmedecins2.sql] (case study).

In [Linux] or [macOS], install [MySQL] or [MariaDB] using the system’s package manager, and then run the scripts using the command-line client [mysql].

docs.title: 13.4. Installing curl
docs.text: [curl] is included with [Windows] 10 and 11, [macOS], and most [Linux] distributions. On [PowerShell], you must type [curl.exe], not [curl]: In older versions of [PowerShell], [curl] is an alias for another command ([Invoke-WebRequest]), which has different options.

docs.title: 8. Authentication and Authorization
docs.text:
Two distinct questions arise for each request:

  • Who is the user? This is authentication: the user has identified themselves with a username and password, and every subsequent request must prove that it comes from them;
  • Do they have permission to access this page? This is authorization: in the case study, only a user with the role ADMIN manages doctors and clients.

Since the server is stateless (Chapter 6), proof of identity must be included with every request. A token JWT ([JSON Web Token]) is used: after login, the server generates a token containing the user’s identity and signs it with a secret key. The token is stored in a cookie; the browser sends it back with every request; the server verifies the signature. The user can read their token but cannot modify it: any modification invalidates the signature.

[NestJS] relies on two libraries for this: [passport] (and its strategy [passport-jwt]), which verifies tokens, and [@nestjs/jwt], which generates them.

The file [src/auth/constants.ts]:

// the name of the cookie that carries the token
export const JWT_COOKIE = 'token';
// the secret key that signs the tokens (in production: an environment variable)
export const JWT_SECRET = process.env.JWT_SECRET ?? 'development-secret';
// lifetime of a token, in seconds
export const JWT_DURATION = 3600;

Line 4: the key that signs the tokens. Anyone who knows this key can generate valid tokens: in production, it comes from an environment variable, never from the source code.

The file [src/auth/users.service.ts]:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import * as bcrypt from 'bcryptjs';

export interface User {
  id: number;
  login: string;
  name: string;
  role: 'ADMIN' | 'USER';
  passwordHash: string; // NEVER the password itself
}

// the users, in memory (the next chapter will put them in a database).
// Each one's password is their login; only its bcrypt hash is kept
@Injectable()
export class UsersService {
  private readonly users: User[] = [
    { id: 1, login: 'admin', name: 'Administrator', role: 'ADMIN', passwordHash: bcrypt.hashSync('admin', 10) },
    { id: 2, login: 'marie', name: 'Marie Pélissier', role: 'USER', passwordHash: bcrypt.hashSync('marie', 10) },
  ];

  byLogin(login: string): User | undefined {
    return this.users.find((u) => u.login === login);
  }
}
  • Line 9: We never store a password; we only store its hash—a fingerprint calculated by a one-way function. We can verify that a password matches a fingerprint, but we cannot recover the password from the fingerprint;
  • Lines 16–19: [bcrypt.hashSync(password, 10)] calculates the hash using the [bcrypt] algorithm. The number 10 represents the “cost”: bcrypt is intentionally slow (2¹⁰ iterations) to discourage anyone from trying millions of passwords. Two hashes of the same password are different (a random “salt” is added): [bcrypt.compare] is responsible for verifying them.

The file [src/auth/auth.service.ts]:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { JwtService } from '@nestjs/jwt';
import * as bcrypt from 'bcryptjs';
import { User, UsersService } from './users.service';

// what the token contains: enough to identify the user without reading the database
export interface TokenContent {
  sub: number; // "subject": the user's identifier (JWT convention)
  login: string;
  name: string;
  role: string;
}

@Injectable()
export class AuthService {
  constructor(
    private readonly users: UsersService,
    private readonly jwt: JwtService,
  ) {}

  // the user if the login / password pair is correct, null otherwise
  async check(login: string, password: string): Promise<User | null> {
    const u = this.users.byLogin(login);
    // bcrypt.compare hashes the typed password and compares the hashes
    return u && (await bcrypt.compare(password, u.passwordHash)) ? u : null;
  }

  // a SIGNED token: the browser can read it, but not modify it
  createToken(u: User): string {
    const content: TokenContent = { sub: u.id, login: u.login, name: u.name, role: u.role };
    return this.jwt.sign(content);
  }
}
  • lines 7–12: the token’s content. [sub] ([subject]) is the conventional name for the user ID. We include whatever the pages need (name, role) so we don’t have to query the database with every request;
  • lines 22–26: verification of the username and password;
  • lines 29–32: [JwtService.sign] generates the signed token. [JwtService] is configured (key, lifetime) in the application module.

The [src/auth/jwt.strategy.ts] file:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PassportStrategy } from '@nestjs/passport';
import { Request } from 'express';
import { ExtractJwt, Strategy } from 'passport-jwt';
import { TokenContent } from './auth.service';
import { JWT_COOKIE, JWT_SECRET } from './constants';

// the logged-in user, as the controllers see it (req.user)
export interface LoggedInUser {
  id: number;
  login: string;
  name: string;
  role: string;
}

// the Passport "jwt" strategy: where to find the token, how to check it
@Injectable()
export class JwtStrategy extends PassportStrategy(Strategy, 'jwt') {
  constructor() {
    super({
      // the token is read from the cookie (and not from the Authorization header)
      jwtFromRequest: ExtractJwt.fromExtractors([(req: Request) => req?.cookies?.[JWT_COOKIE] ?? null]),
      ignoreExpiration: false, // an expired token is rejected
      secretOrKey: JWT_SECRET, // to check the signature
    });
  }

  // called if the token is valid; what it returns becomes req.user
  validate(content: TokenContent): LoggedInUser {
    return { id: content.sub, login: content.login, name: content.name, role: content.role };
  }
}
  • line 18: a [Passport] strategy, named [jwt], describes how to authenticate a request;
  • line 22: where to find the token: in the cookie. (A [JavaScript] client would instead send it in the [Authorization: Bearer ...] header; see [ExtractJwt.fromAuthHeaderAsBearerToken()]);
  • lines 23–24: an expired or incorrectly signed token is rejected;
  • lines 29–31: called when the token is valid. The result is [req.user]: the logged-in user, with access to actions.

The file [src/auth/jwt-auth.guard.ts]:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AuthGuard } from '@nestjs/passport';

// the guard that runs the 'jwt' strategy: no valid token -> 401
@Injectable()
export class JwtAuthGuard extends AuthGuard('jwt') {}

[AuthGuard('jwt')] creates a guard that executes the [jwt] strategy. Without a valid token, it raises a [UnauthorizedException] (401).

The file [src/auth/auth.controller.ts]:

import { Body, Controller, Get, Post, Render, Res } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Response } from 'express';
import { AuthService } from './auth.service';
import { JWT_COOKIE, JWT_DURATION } from './constants';

@Controller()
export class AuthController {
  constructor(private readonly auth: AuthService) {}

  @Get('login')
  @Render('login')
  form(): object {
    return {};
  }

  @Post('login')
  async logIn(@Body() body: { login?: string; password?: string }, @Res() res: Response): Promise<void> {
    const user = await this.auth.check(body.login ?? '', body.password ?? '');
    if (!user) {
      // deliberately vague message: we do not say which of the two is wrong
      res.render('login', { login: body.login, error: 'Incorrect login or password.' });
      return;
    }
    // the token is put in an httpOnly cookie: the page's JavaScript
    // cannot read it, the browser sends it back with each request
    res.cookie(JWT_COOKIE, this.auth.createToken(user), {
      httpOnly: true,
      sameSite: 'lax',
      maxAge: JWT_DURATION * 1000,
    });
    res.redirect('/profile');
  }

  // logging out MODIFIES the state: it is a POST, not a link
  @Post('logout')
  logOut(@Res() res: Response): void {
    res.clearCookie(JWT_COOKIE);
    res.redirect('/login');
  }
}
  • lines 17–32: the login. If the login fails, the form is redisplayed with a deliberately vague message: stating “this login does not exist” would help an attacker find valid logins;
  • lines 26–30: if successful, the token is stored in an [httpOnly] cookie; the page’s [JavaScript] cannot read it, which protects the token if a malicious script were to execute on the page. [sameSite: 'lax']: The cookie is not included in POST requests sent from another site, which protects against request forgery ([CSRF]);
  • Lines 35–39: Logging out deletes the cookie. This is a POST: it changes the user’s status (see Example 21).

The [src/profile.controller.ts] file:

import { Controller, Get, Render, Req, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Request } from 'express';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from './auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { LoggedInUser } from './auth/jwt.strategy';

@Controller()
export class ProfileController {
  // public page
  @Get()
  @Render('home')
  home(): object {
    return {};
  }

  // protected page: the guard requires a valid token
  @Get('profile')
  @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
  @Render('profile')
  profile(@Req() req: Request): object {
    return { user: req.user as LoggedInUser };
  }
}

Line 17: The page [/profile] is protected by the guard. The action reads the user from [req.user].

The file [src/errors.filter.ts]:

import { ArgumentsHost, Catch, ExceptionFilter, HttpException, HttpStatus } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Response } from 'express';

@Catch(HttpException)
export class ErrorsFilter implements ExceptionFilter {
  catch(exception: HttpException, host: ArgumentsHost): void {
    const res = host.switchToHttp().getResponse<Response>();
    const status = exception.getStatus();
    // 401 (no token, or invalid token): off to the login page
    if (status === HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED) {
      res.redirect('/login');
      return;
    }
    res.status(status).render('error', { status, message: exception.message });
  }
}

Lines 10–13: A 401 error does not display an error page; the user is redirected to the login page.

The file [src/app.module.ts]:

import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { JwtModule } from '@nestjs/jwt';
import { PassportModule } from '@nestjs/passport';
import { AuthController } from './auth/auth.controller';
import { AuthService } from './auth/auth.service';
import { JWT_DURATION, JWT_SECRET } from './auth/constants';
import { JwtStrategy } from './auth/jwt.strategy';
import { UsersService } from './auth/users.service';
import { ProfileController } from './profile.controller';

@Module({
  imports: [
    PassportModule,
    // JwtService, configured once and for all: key and lifetime
    JwtModule.register({ secret: JWT_SECRET, signOptions: { expiresIn: JWT_DURATION } }),
  ],
  controllers: [AuthController, ProfileController],
  providers: [UsersService, AuthService, JwtStrategy],
})
export class AppModule {}

Line 15: the configuration of [JwtService]: token key and lifetime (one hour).

docs.title: 8.1.1. Execution
docs.text:
Without a cookie, the protected page redirects to the login page:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/profile

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /login
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 28

Found. Redirecting to /login

An incorrect password:

Successful login, as seen by [curl]:

curl -i -c cookies.txt -d "login=marie&password=marie" http://localhost:3000/login

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Set-Cookie: token=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOjIsImxvZ2luIjoibWFyaWUiLCJuYW1lIjoiTWFyaWUgUMOpbGlzc2llciIsInJvbGUiOiJVU0VSIiwiaWF0IjoxNzkwMTczMDg3LCJleHAiOjE3OTAxNzY2ODd9.LoujmLAq__cPbevACUDUMvdPHkH7r_ekv48IwHqc3Dk; Max-Age=3600; Path=/; Expires=Wed, 23 Sep 2026 15:18:07 GMT; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Location: /profile
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 30

Found. Redirecting to /profile

The token consists of three parts separated by periods: a header, the content, and the signature. The first two are simply encoded as [base64url]; let’s decode the content:

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOjIsImxvZ2luIjoibWFyaWUiLCJuYW1lIjoiTWFyaWUgUMOpbGlzc2llciIsInJvbGUiOiJVU0VSIiwiaWF0IjoxNzkwMTczMDg3LCJleHAiOjE3OTAxNzY2ODd9.LoujmLAq__cPbevACUDUMvdPHkH7r_ekv48IwHqc3Dk

{"sub": 2, "login": "marie", "name": "Marie Pélissier", "role": "USER", "iat": 1790173087, "exp": 1790176687}

The content generated by [createToken] is included, along with two fields added by [JwtService]: [iat] ([issued at], the creation date) and [exp] (the expiration date), in seconds since January 1, 1970. The token is not encrypted: it does not contain any confidential information. In the browser:

Now let’s try to modify the token to assign ourselves the role ADMIN: we decode the content, replace [USER] with [ADMIN], and re-encode it… but we can’t recalculate the signature without the secret key:

curl -i -b "token=eyJhbGciOi...(modified content)...LoujmLAq..." http://localhost:3000/profile

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /login
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 28

Found. Redirecting to /login

The signature no longer matches the content: the token is rejected (error 401), and the exception handler redirects to the login page. Logging out:

curl -i -b cookies.txt -X POST http://localhost:3000/logout

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Set-Cookie: token=; Path=/; Expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT
Location: /login
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 28

Found. Redirecting to /login

docs.title: 8.2. Example 26: Roles
docs.text:
Example 26 builds on Example 25 and adds a page reserved for the role ADMIN. Three new files have been added.

The file [src/auth/roles.decorator.ts]:

import { SetMetadata } from '@nestjs/common';

export const ROLES_KEY = 'roles';

// @Roles('ADMIN'): puts a METADATA on the action (or the controller);
// the decorator checks nothing itself, RolesGuard is the one that will read it
export const Roles = (...roles: string[]) => SetMetadata(ROLES_KEY, roles);

Line 7: [SetMetadata] attaches metadata (any information) to the decorated class or method. [@Roles('ADMIN')] does not check anything: it declares the required role.

The file [src/auth/roles.guard.ts]:

import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, ForbiddenException, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Reflector } from '@nestjs/core';
import { Request } from 'express';
import { LoggedInUser } from './jwt.strategy';
import { ROLES_KEY } from './roles.decorator';

@Injectable()
export class RolesGuard implements CanActivate {
  // Reflector: the NestJS tool to read the metadata back
  constructor(private readonly reflector: Reflector) {}

  canActivate(context: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    // @Roles of the action, failing that the one of the controller
    const required = this.reflector.getAllAndOverride<string[]>(ROLES_KEY, [context.getHandler(), context.getClass()]);
    if (!required || required.length === 0) {
      return true; // no @Roles: no role restriction
    }
    // req.user was set by JwtAuthGuard, which runs BEFORE this guard
    const user = context.switchToHttp().getRequest<Request>().user as LoggedInUser;
    if (!required.includes(user.role)) {
      throw new ForbiddenException(`the ${user.role} role does not give access to this page`);
    }
    return true;
  }
}
  • line 10: [Reflector] is the service for [NestJS] that reads the metadata;
  • line 14: the roles required by the action, or failing that, by its controller. This is where the guard’s execution context comes into play (see Chapter 7);
  • lines 15–17: without [@Roles], there are no restrictions;
  • line 19: [req.user] was registered by the guard [JwtAuthGuard], which executes before it;
  • lines 20–22: an insufficient role causes a 403 (Forbidden) error.

The file [src/admin.controller.ts]:

import { Controller, Get, Render, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from './auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { Roles } from './auth/roles.decorator';
import { RolesGuard } from './auth/roles.guard';

// the order matters: first WHO is it (JwtAuthGuard), then IS IT ALLOWED (RolesGuard)
@Controller('admin')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard, RolesGuard)
@Roles('ADMIN')
export class AdminController {
  @Get()
  @Render('admin')
  admin(): object {
    return {};
  }
}

lines 8–9: guards are executed in the order in which they are listed: first the identification, then the role check. The entire controller is reserved for the role ADMIN. The user [marie] (role USER) attempts to open the administration page:

Same attempt by [admin]:

The case study has three roles (ADMIN, DOCTOR, USER) and uses exactly these two guards. The exception filter converts the 403 into a translated error page.

docs.title: 8.3. Example 27: CAPTCHA and attempt limits
docs.text:
A login page attracts bots: programs that try thousands of login/password combinations. Two complementary safeguards:

  • a CAPTCHA: an image of distorted characters that a human can read easily but that a simple bot cannot decipher;
  • an attempt limit: after a few failed attempts, the address IP is blocked for a while.

Example 27 adds these two safeguards to Example 25.

The file [src/auth/captcha.service.ts]:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { randomUUID } from 'crypto';
import * as svgCaptcha from 'svg-captcha';

export interface Captcha {
  id: string; // placed in a hidden field of the form
  svg: string; // the image, inserted as is into the page
}

@Injectable()
export class CaptchaService {
  // id -> expected answer. The answer NEVER leaves the server
  private readonly answers = new Map<string, string>();

  generate(): Captcha {
    // svg-captcha: a random text, drawn with distorted characters
    const { text, data } = svgCaptcha.create({ size: 5, noise: 3, color: true, ignoreChars: '0oO1iIlL' });
    const id = randomUUID();
    this.answers.set(id, text.toLowerCase());
    return { id, svg: data };
  }

  // is the answer the right one? In all cases, the captcha is
  // consumed: an image is used only once
  check(id: unknown, input: unknown): boolean {
    if (typeof id !== 'string' || typeof input !== 'string') {
      return false;
    }
    const expected = this.answers.get(id);
    this.answers.delete(id);
    return expected !== undefined && expected === input.trim().toLowerCase();
  }
}
  • Line 13: The expected responses are stored by the server under a random identifier. The page contains only the image and the identifier: the response never leaves the server;
  • lines 15–21: The [svg-captcha] library generates a random text string and renders it as an image (SVG), obscured by lines. Characters that are easily confused (0 and O, 1 and l, etc.) are excluded;
  • lines 25–32: The verification process consumes the CAPTCHA: an image is used only once; a bot cannot reuse a response it has already found.

The file [src/auth/limiter.service.ts]:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';

const MAX_FAILURES = 3; // tolerated failures...
const BLOCK_MS = 60 * 1000; // ... before a one-minute block

// limits the number of login attempts per IP address
@Injectable()
export class LimiterService {
  private readonly counters = new Map<string, { failures: number; blockedUntil: number }>();

  // 0 if the IP may try its luck, otherwise the number of seconds to wait
  blockedSeconds(ip: string): number {
    const c = this.counters.get(ip);
    const remaining = c ? c.blockedUntil - Date.now() : 0;
    return remaining > 0 ? Math.ceil(remaining / 1000) : 0;
  }

  failure(ip: string): void {
    const c = this.counters.get(ip) ?? { failures: 0, blockedUntil: 0 };
    c.failures++;
    if (c.failures >= MAX_FAILURES) {
      c.blockedUntil = Date.now() + BLOCK_MS;
      c.failures = 0;
    }
    this.counters.set(ip, c);
  }

  success(ip: string): void {
    this.counters.delete(ip);
  }
}
  • lines 3–4: Three failures block the address IP for one minute;
  • lines 12–16: the remaining block time;
  • lines 18–26 and 28–30: a failure is counted; a success resets the counter to zero.

The file [src/auth/auth.controller.ts]:

import { Body, Controller, Get, Ip, Post, Res } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Response } from 'express';
import { AuthService } from './auth.service';
import { CaptchaService } from './captcha.service';
import { JWT_COOKIE, JWT_DURATION } from './constants';
import { LimiterService } from './limiter.service';

interface LoginBody {
  login?: string;
  password?: string;
  captchaId?: string;
  captcha?: string;
}

@Controller()
export class AuthController {
  constructor(
    private readonly auth: AuthService,
    private readonly captchas: CaptchaService,
    private readonly limiter: LimiterService,
  ) {}

  @Get('login')
  form(@Res() res: Response): void {
    this.display(res, {});
  }

  @Post('login')
  async logIn(@Body() body: LoginBody, @Ip() ip: string, @Res() res: Response): Promise<void> {
    // 1. a blocked IP is not even listened to
    const seconds = this.limiter.blockedSeconds(ip);
    if (seconds > 0) {
      this.display(res, { login: body.login, error: `Too many attempts: try again in ${seconds} s.` });
      return;
    }
    // 2. the captcha, then 3. the login and the password
    const captchaOk = this.captchas.check(body.captchaId, body.captcha);
    const user = captchaOk ? await this.auth.check(body.login ?? '', body.password ?? '') : null;
    if (!user) {
      this.limiter.failure(ip);
      const error = captchaOk ? 'Incorrect login or password.' : 'The copied characters are incorrect.';
      this.display(res, { login: body.login, error });
      return;
    }
    this.limiter.success(ip);
    res.cookie(JWT_COOKIE, this.auth.createToken(user), {
      httpOnly: true,
      sameSite: 'lax',
      maxAge: JWT_DURATION * 1000,
    });
    res.redirect('/profile');
  }

  @Post('logout')
  logOut(@Res() res: Response): void {
    res.clearCookie(JWT_COOKIE);
    res.redirect('/login');
  }

  // each display of the form has a NEW captcha
  private display(res: Response, model: object): void {
    res.render('login', { ...model, captcha: this.captchas.generate() });
  }
}
  • line 29: [@Ip()] injects the client’s address IP;
  • lines 32–35: a blocked IP is not even processed;
  • lines 37–38: the CAPTCHA is verified first; the password (which requires a computationally expensive bcrypt calculation) is only checked if the CAPTCHA is correct;
  • lines 39–44: an incorrect CAPTCHA counts as a failure;
  • lines 61–63: each time the form is displayed, a new CAPTCHA is generated.

docs.title: 11.1. The Problem
docs.text:
The RdvMedecins application manages appointments for a medical practice. Each doctor has time slots (from 8:00 AM to 12:00 PM in 20-minute increments, for example); an appointment consists of a day, a time slot, and a client (a patient). It uses the database and business layers from the [NestJS] server in the courses “An Example of a Flutter Client/Server / NestJS” and “An Example of an Angular Client/Server / NestJS, and displays the same pages as the [Angular] client; but instead of serving JSON to a client [JavaScript] or [Flutter], it generates its own HTML pages.

Three user roles share the application:

RoleWhoWhat they can doADMINThe administrator ([admin])view schedules, make and cancel appointments for any patient; manage (list, add, edit, delete) doctors and clientsDOCTORDoctorsView schedules, book, and cancel appointments for any patientUSERclients (patients)view schedules without seeing other patients’ names; book an appointment for themselves; cancel their appointment; manage their account; create an account

Key management rules:

  • No appointments in the past;
  • a time slot can only be booked once per day;
  • a patient may have only one upcoming appointment at a time;
  • Two doctors (or two clients) cannot have the same first and last names, and a login belongs to only one account;
  • A doctor with appointments cannot be deleted; A client is deleted along with their appointments;
  • the login page is protected against bots (CAPTCHA, limited attempts), and creating a client account requires first solving the CAPTCHA on that page.

A patient (role USER) arrives at My area: their upcoming appointment, which they can cancel, and links to their account management and calendar:

In the calendar, they see their own appointment, but not the names of other patients (Booked). Since they already have an upcoming appointment, they cannot schedule another one:

A patient without an appointment can book an available time slot for themselves:

docs.title: 11.4. Application Architecture
docs.text:
• [src/main.ts] configures the application: view engine, static files, cookies, exception filter;
  • [src/auth]: authentication, tokens (JWT), roles, CAPTCHA, and attempt limits;
  • [src/web]: the web layer. Its controllers ([src/web/controllers]) all pass through a single service, [ApplicationModelService], which stores the lists of doctors and clients in memory and forwards other requests to the business layer;
  • [src/business]: the business rules;
  • [src/repositories]: the DAO layer, one class per table;
  • [src/entities]: the entities [TypeORM]; [src/domain]: the calendar objects, calculated by the business layer;
  • [views]: the views [Handlebars]; [i18n]: the dictionaries; [public]: the style sheet and the page script.

The suite comments on all files, from the lower layers (database) to the upper layers (views).

docs.title: 11.5. The database
docs.text:
The file [database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql]:

-- =========================================================================
-- Database [dbrdvmedecins2] - MySQL 8
--
-- Evolution of [dbrdvmedecins]:
--   1. the [doctors] and [clients] tables get a [user] column,
--      foreign key to users(id): every doctor and every client is
--      now also a user able to log in;
--   2. a third role appears: DOCTOR (in addition to ADMIN and USER);
--   3. the script creates a [users] row for each doctor (role DOCTOR)
--      and for each client (role USER):
--        - login        = last name in lower case
--        - password     = last name in lower case, hashed with bcrypt (10 rounds)
--        - display name = first name + last name
--
--   4. uniqueness constraints, all NAMED (the NestJS application recognizes
--      the name of the violated constraint in the MySQL error message):
--        - unq_users_login                   : a login belongs to one account only;
--        - unq_doctors_first_name_last_name  : two doctors cannot have the
--                                              same first and last names;
--        - unq_clients_first_name_last_name  : same for the clients.
--      Beware: the utf8mb4_unicode_ci collation compares regardless of
--      case and accents - "Hélène DUPONT" and "helene dupont"
--      are therefore considered identical.
--
-- The [users] table must now be created BEFORE [doctors] and [clients]
-- (they reference it), and dropped AFTER them.
-- =========================================================================

-- we start again from an empty database on each run of the script (handy in development)
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS dbrdvmedecins2 CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbrdvmedecins2;

-- drop order: from the "child" tables to the "parent" tables
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS appointments;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS slots;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS clients;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS doctors;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users;

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [users]: the users allowed to log in to the application
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE users (
  id       INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version  INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  login    VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,                 -- login identifier
  password VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,                -- HASHED password (bcrypt) - never in clear
  name     VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,                 -- name displayed once logged in
  role     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,                 -- 'ADMIN', 'DOCTOR' or 'USER'
  -- a login can belong to one account only
  CONSTRAINT unq_users_login UNIQUE (login)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [doctors]: the doctors of the practice
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE doctors (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,   -- primary key (technical identifier)
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,            -- row version number (optimistic lock)
  title      VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,              -- Melle, Mme, Mr
  last_name  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  first_name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  `user`     INT NOT NULL,                      -- foreign key -> users(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_doctors_user FOREIGN KEY (`user`) REFERENCES users(id),
  -- one account per doctor, and one doctor per account
  CONSTRAINT unq_doctors_user UNIQUE (`user`),
  -- two doctors cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_doctors_first_name_last_name UNIQUE (first_name, last_name)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [clients]: the doctors' patients
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE clients (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  title      VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,
  last_name  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  first_name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  `user`     INT NOT NULL,                      -- foreign key -> users(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_clients_user FOREIGN KEY (`user`) REFERENCES users(id),
  -- one account per client, and one client per account
  CONSTRAINT unq_clients_user UNIQUE (`user`),
  -- two clients cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_clients_first_name_last_name UNIQUE (first_name, last_name)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [slots]: the time slots of each doctor
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE slots (
  id           INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version      INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  doctor_id    INT NOT NULL,                     -- foreign key -> doctors(id)
  start_hour   INT NOT NULL,                     -- start hour of the slot
  start_minute INT NOT NULL,                     -- start minute of the slot
  end_hour     INT NOT NULL,                     -- end hour of the slot
  end_minute   INT NOT NULL,                     -- end minute of the slot
  CONSTRAINT fk_slots_doctor FOREIGN KEY (doctor_id) REFERENCES doctors(id)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [appointments]: the appointments booked by the clients
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE appointments (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  day        DATE NOT NULL,                      -- day of the appointment
  slot_id    INT NOT NULL,                       -- foreign key -> slots(id)
  client_id  INT NOT NULL,                       -- foreign key -> clients(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_appointments_slot   FOREIGN KEY (slot_id)   REFERENCES slots(id),
  CONSTRAINT fk_appointments_client FOREIGN KEY (client_id) REFERENCES clients(id),
  -- the same slot, on the same day, can be booked only once
  CONSTRAINT unq1_appointments UNIQUE (day, slot_id)
);

-- =========================================================================
-- Demo data
-- =========================================================================

-- the users: passwords hashed with bcrypt (10 salt rounds)
--   admin/admin (ADMIN)
--   one DOCTOR account per doctor, one USER account per client
--   (the user/user demo account is gone: a USER account is
--   now ALWAYS a client's account, who can book and manage the account)
--   (login = password = last name in lower case)

Let’s comment on this script:

  • line 30: as in Example 28, the collation [utf8mb4_unicode_ci] ignores uppercase letters and accents in comparisons;
  • lines 34–38: tables are deleted from the “child” tables to the “parent” tables: a table referenced by a foreign key cannot be deleted before the tables that reference it;
  • lines 43–52: user accounts. [password] contains the bcrypt hash of the password (see Example 25). Line 51: a login is unique;
  • Lines 57–69: Doctors. Each has an account (column [user], foreign key to [users], line 64). The name [user] is a reserved word for [MySQL]: it is enclosed in backticks. Line 66: an account belongs to only one doctor; line 68: no two doctors can have the same first and last names;
  • lines 74–86: clients, following the same format;
  • lines 91–100: each doctor’s time slots (start and end times in hours and minutes);
  • lines 105–115: appointments: one day, one time slot, one client. Line 114: a time slot is reserved only once per day;
  • lines 127–137: demo accounts; each account’s password is its login;
  • lines 141–144: each doctor’s [user] column is retrieved via a subquery on the login, rather than assuming the generated credentials;
  • lines 167–168: a same-day appointment ([CURDATE()]), to immediately show a booked time slot.

// =========================================================================
// config/database.config.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Configuration of the connection to the MySQL database, used by
// TypeORM. It is the equivalent of the [DomainAndPersitenceConfig] class of the
// original Spring project, which defined a [DataSource] (@Bean block).
//
// Here, no class: NestJS/TypeORM prefers a simple function that
// returns a configuration object, read from the environment variables
// (.env file at the project root, loaded automatically by NestJS
// through the @nestjs/config module if installed - here we read
// process.env directly to stay simple and educational).
// =========================================================================

import { TypeOrmModuleOptions } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Doctor } from '../entities/doctor.entity';
import { Client } from '../entities/client.entity';
import { Slot } from '../entities/slot.entity';
import { Appointment } from '../entities/appointment.entity';
import { User } from '../entities/user.entity';

export function getDatabaseConfig(): TypeOrmModuleOptions {
  return {
    // 'mysql': we use the MySQL driver, like the original project (MySQL5 -> MySQL8 here).
    type: 'mysql',
    host: process.env.DB_HOST ?? 'localhost',
    port: process.env.DB_PORT ? parseInt(process.env.DB_PORT, 10) : 3306,
    username: process.env.DB_USERNAME ?? 'root',
    password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD ?? '',
    database: process.env.DB_DATABASE ?? 'dbrdvmedecins2',

    // the list of entities (@Entity classes) that TypeORM must manage.
    // It is the equivalent of the automatic "scan" of @Entity classes done by Spring Boot.
    entities: [Doctor, Client, Slot, Appointment, User],

    // IMPORTANT: synchronize=false at all times in this course.
    // If synchronize were true, TypeORM would modify the database schema on its own
    // from the entities: handy for a throwaway prototype, dangerous as soon as there is
    // real data (risk of data loss). Like a real team would, we prefer
    // to keep control of the schema through the database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql script.
    synchronize: false,

    // displays the SQL queries generated by TypeORM in the console: very useful to
    // understand what the ORM does for you, exactly like the Hibernate logs
    // of the original Spring project.
    logging: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production',
  };
}

docs.title: 11.7. Starting the application
docs.text:
The file [src/main.ts]:

// =========================================================================
// main.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Entry point of the application. Compared with the JSON server, the
// startup also configures everything needed to BUILD HTML PAGES
// on the server side:
//   - a view engine (Handlebars, files views/*.hbs);
//   - the static files (Bootstrap, CSS, a little JavaScript);
//   - cookie parsing (JWT token, language, flash messages);
//   - a filter that turns errors into HTML pages.
// There is no CORS to allow any more: pages and data now come from
// the SAME server.
// =========================================================================

import 'dotenv/config'; // MUST remain the very first import (see JSON server)
import 'reflect-metadata';
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { NestExpressApplication } from '@nestjs/platform-express';
import * as cookieParser from 'cookie-parser';
import * as hbs from 'hbs';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';
import { BOOTSTRAP_DIR, PARTIALS_DIR, PUBLIC_DIR, VIEWS_DIR } from './config/paths';
import { registerHelpers } from './web/views/handlebars-helpers';
import { viewContextMiddleware } from './web/view-context';
import { HtmlExceptionFilter } from './web/html-exception.filter';
import { ViewUserInterceptor } from './web/view-user.interceptor';

async function bootstrap() {
  // NestExpressApplication: we state that the underlying platform is
  // Express, to get access to its own methods (setViewEngine,
  // useStaticAssets...) - they do not exist for the Fastify platform.
  const app = await NestFactory.create<NestExpressApplication>(AppModule);

  // 1. static files: /css/..., /js/... (public/ folder) and
  //    /bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css (directly from node_modules:
  //    no need to copy Bootstrap into the project)
  app.useStaticAssets(PUBLIC_DIR);
  app.useStaticAssets(BOOTSTRAP_DIR, { prefix: '/bootstrap/' });

  // 2. the view engine. The views/layout.hbs file is used
  //    AUTOMATICALLY by hbs as the common template of all pages:
  //    each view is inserted at the {{{body}}} spot of this template.
  app.setBaseViewsDir(VIEWS_DIR);
  app.setViewEngine('hbs');
  registerHelpers(hbs);
  // the "partials" (views/partials/*.hbs): reusable pieces of page,
  // inserted with {{> name}}. registerPartials reads the folder
  // asynchronously: we wait until it is done before accepting requests.
  await new Promise<void>((done) => hbs.registerPartials(PARTIALS_DIR, () => done()));

  // 3. cookie-parser fills req.cookies; then our middleware prepares the
  //    language and the flash message of each page (see web/view-context.ts)
  app.use(cookieParser());
  app.use(viewContextMiddleware);

  // 4. the logged-in user, visible to all views; and the errors
  //    turned into HTML pages (or into a redirect to /login)
  app.useGlobalInterceptors(new ViewUserInterceptor());
  app.useGlobalFilters(new HtmlExceptionFilter());

  const port = process.env.PORT ? parseInt(process.env.PORT, 10) : 8081;
  await app.listen(port);
  // eslint-disable-next-line no-console
  console.log(`[RdvMedecins] web application started on http://localhost:${port}`);
}

bootstrap();

Let’s break down this code:

  • Line 15: [dotenv/config] reads the file [.env] and places its values into [process.env]. This import must be the first one: the other modules read [process.env] as soon as they are loaded ([JWT_SECRET], for example);
  • lines 37–38: static files (see Example 15);
  • lines 43–49: the view engine, helpers, and partial views (see Examples 15 and 16);
  • lines 53–54: reading cookies, followed by the middleware that prepares the language and flash message for each page (see [web/view-context.ts]);
  • lines 58–59: a global interceptor exposes the logged-in user to the views, and a global filter converts exceptions into HTML pages (see Chapter 7);
  • line 61: the port, read from [.env] (8081 by default).

The [src/app.module.ts] file:

// =========================================================================
// app.module.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The root module. Same layers as the JSON server (DAO, business,
// cache/facade); only the controllers change: they now build
// HTML pages instead of JSON responses.
// =========================================================================

import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { TypeOrmModule } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { getDatabaseConfig } from './config/database.config';

import { Doctor } from './entities/doctor.entity';
import { Client } from './entities/client.entity';
import { Slot } from './entities/slot.entity';
import { Appointment } from './entities/appointment.entity';

import { DoctorRepository } from './repositories/doctor.repository';
import { ClientRepository } from './repositories/client.repository';
import { SlotRepository } from './repositories/slot.repository';
import { AppointmentRepository } from './repositories/appointment.repository';

import { BUSINESS_TOKEN } from './business/business.interface';
import { BusinessService } from './business/business.service';

import { ApplicationModelService } from './web/application-model.service';
import { ScheduleController } from './web/controllers/schedule.controller';
import { DoctorsController } from './web/controllers/doctors.controller';
import { ClientsController } from './web/controllers/clients.controller';
import { LanguageController } from './web/controllers/language.controller';
import { RegistrationController } from './web/controllers/registration.controller';
import { PatientAreaController } from './web/controllers/patient-area.controller';

import { AuthModule } from './auth/auth.module';

@Module({
  imports: [
    TypeOrmModule.forRoot(getDatabaseConfig()),
    TypeOrmModule.forFeature([Doctor, Client, Slot, Appointment]),
    // AuthModule provides /login and /logout; it exports UserRepository
    // (injected into BusinessService), AuthService, CaptchaService and
    // AttemptLimiterService (injected into the controllers of src/web/)
    AuthModule,
  ],
  controllers: [
    ScheduleController,
    DoctorsController,
    ClientsController,
    LanguageController,
    RegistrationController, // "Create a patient account" (public)
    PatientAreaController, // "My area", "Manage my account" (USER)
  ],
  providers: [
    DoctorRepository,
    ClientRepository,
    SlotRepository,
    AppointmentRepository,
    { provide: BUSINESS_TOKEN, useClass: BusinessService },
    ApplicationModelService,
  ],
})
export class AppModule {}

  • line 43: the authentication module, with its own controller and services;
  • lines 45–52: the web layer controllers;
  • Lines 53–60: the services: the DAO layer (the four repositories), the business layer, and the web layer cache. Line 58: The business layer is registered under a token ([BUSINESS_TOKEN]) rather than under the name of its class: those who use it depend on the [IBusiness] interface, not on the [BusinessService] class. The implementation could be replaced (with a test version, for example) by modifying only this line.

docs.title: 11.8. The entities
docs.text: The [TypeORM] entities map to the database tables and classes in [TypeScript] (see Example 28). Their comments often refer to the [Java] / [Spring] project, of which the application is a distant descendant, and to the “JSON server”: the [NestJS] server from the client/server courses, whose case study incorporates the DAO and business layers.

docs.title: 11.8.1. src/entities/abstract.entity.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// entities/abstract.entity.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Equivalent of the [AbstractEntity] class of the original Spring project,
// which was annotated @MappedSuperclass. It groups the two fields
// common to all our persistent entities: the identifier [id] and the
// version number [version] used to manage concurrent access.
//
// In JPA, @MappedSuperclass means "this class is not a table,
// but its fields must be added to the tables of the child classes".
// TypeORM offers exactly the same mechanism: it is enough for an abstract
// class (not decorated with @Entity) to be inherited by a class which,
// itself, carries the @Entity annotation. TypeORM then automatically adds
// the inherited columns to the table of the child class.
// =========================================================================

import { PrimaryGeneratedColumn, VersionColumn } from 'typeorm';

export abstract class AbstractEntity {
  // equivalent of:
  //   @Id
  //   @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.AUTO)
  //   protected Long id;
  //
  // @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() declares a primary key auto-incremented by the DBMS,
  // exactly as GenerationType.AUTO delegated it to the DBMS.
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn()
  id: number;

  // equivalent of:
  //   @Version
  //   protected Long version;
  //
  // @VersionColumn() is THE native TypeORM mechanism for optimistic locking:
  // TypeORM automatically increments this column on each UPDATE, and throws an error
  // when trying to save an entity whose version no longer matches the one in the
  // database (someone else changed it in the meantime). It maps directly to the
  // role of @Version in JPA/Hibernate.
  @VersionColumn()
  version: number;
}
  • line 19: an abstract class without a decorator [@Entity]: it does not correspond to any table, but its columns are added to those of the child classes;
  • lines 27–28: the primary key, generated by the database;
  • lines 39–40: the row version, incremented by [TypeORM] with each modification (optimistic lock; see Example 28).

docs.title: 11.8.2. src/entities/person.entity.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// entities/person.entity.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Parent class (not persisted itself) of the [Doctor] and
// [Client] entities: a title, a last name, a first name - and, new in the
// [dbrdvmedecins2] database, the associated user account ([user] column).
//
// A relation declared in an abstract class is inherited by the
// child classes exactly like the columns: TypeORM therefore adds the
// [user] relation to the [doctors] table AND to the [clients] table.
// =========================================================================

import { Column, JoinColumn, OneToOne, RelationId } from 'typeorm';
import { AbstractEntity } from './abstract.entity';
import { User } from './user.entity';

export abstract class Person extends AbstractEntity {
  @Column({ length: 5 })
  title: string; // Melle, Mme, Mr

  @Column({ name: 'last_name', length: 20 })
  lastName: string;

  @Column({ name: 'first_name', length: 20 })
  firstName: string;

  // @OneToOne: a doctor (or a client) has ONE user account, and a
  // user account belongs to at most ONE person (the [user] column
  // is declared UNIQUE in the SQL script).
  // @JoinColumn({ name: 'user' }): it is THIS table (doctors / clients)
  // that carries the foreign key, in the column named [user].
  // As for the other relations, [user] is only loaded on request
  // (`relations` option) - see doctor.repository.ts.
  @OneToOne(() => User)
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'user' })
  user: User;

  // the raw value of the foreign key, without loading the full User
  // (same technique as Slot.doctorId, see slot.entity.ts)
  @RelationId((person: Person) => person.user)
  userId: number;
}
  • line 17: the parent class of [Doctor] and [Client], itself a child of [AbstractEntity];
  • Lines 18–25: title, last name, first name;
  • lines 34–36: a one-to-one relationship to the user account. [@JoinColumn] indicates that this table contains the foreign key, in column [user]. The relationship is loaded only if requested (option [relations] in queries);
  • Lines 40–41: [@RelationId] exposes the value of the foreign key (the account ID) without loading the account itself.

docs.title: 11.8.3. src/entities/doctor.entity.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// entities/doctor.entity.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Equivalent of the JPA entity [Medecin] (a doctor):
//
//   @Entity
//   @Table(name = "medecins")
//   public class Medecin extends Personne { ... }
// =========================================================================

import { Entity, OneToMany, Unique } from 'typeorm';
import { Person } from './person.entity';
import { Slot } from './slot.entity';

// @Entity({ name: 'doctors' }): declares the class as a TypeORM entity,
// persisted in the [doctors] table. It is the exact equivalent of
// @Entity + @Table(name = "doctors") in JPA.
@Entity({ name: 'doctors' })
// reminder of the SQL constraint of the database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql script: two
// doctors cannot have the same first and last names. As for unq1_appointments
// (see appointment.entity.ts), it is documentation: synchronize=false, it is the
// SQL script that really creates the constraint - with THIS name, which the
// business layer recognizes in MySQL error messages (see business.service.ts).
@Unique('unq_doctors_first_name_last_name', ['firstName', 'lastName'])
export class Doctor extends Person {
  // inverse relation (optional, handy to navigate from a doctor to the doctor's slots).
  // The original project did not define it on the [Medecin] side (only on the [Creneau] side),
  // but TypeORM makes it almost free to add and it is educationally useful:
  // it shows the relation "1 doctor -> several slots" in both directions.
  @OneToMany(() => Slot, (slot) => slot.doctor)
  slots: Slot[];
}
  • line 18: the class corresponds to the table [doctors];
  • line 24: the uniqueness constraint, included here for documentation purposes; it is actually created by the script SQL ([synchronize: false]);
  • Lines 30–31: the one-to-many relationship to the doctor’s time slots, the inverse of the relationship [@ManyToOne] from [Slot].

// =========================================================================
// entities/client.entity.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Equivalent of the JPA entity [Client]:
//
//   @Entity
//   @Table(name = "clients")
//   public class Client extends Personne { ... }
//
// Beware: [Client] here means a PATIENT of the medical practice, not an
// HTTP client! It is the vocabulary of the original business domain, kept
// as is to remain faithful to the source document.
// =========================================================================

import { Entity, Unique } from 'typeorm';
import { Person } from './person.entity';

@Entity({ name: 'clients' })
// two clients cannot have the same first and last names
// (see the same constraint on Doctor, doctor.entity.ts)
@Unique('unq_clients_first_name_last_name', ['firstName', 'lastName'])

A client (a patient): a [Person] from the [clients] table, with no additional fields.

docs.title: 11.8.5. src/entities/slot.entity.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// entities/slot.entity.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Equivalent of the JPA entity [Creneau] (a time slot):
//
//   @Entity
//   @Table(name = "creneaux")
//   public class Creneau extends AbstractEntity {
//       private int hdebut, mdebut, hfin, mfin;
//       @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
//       @JoinColumn(name = "id_medecin")
//       private Medecin medecin;
//       @Column(name = "id_medecin", insertable = false, updatable = false)
//       private long idMedecin;
//   }
// =========================================================================

import { Column, Entity, JoinColumn, ManyToOne, RelationId } from 'typeorm';
import { AbstractEntity } from './abstract.entity';
import { Doctor } from './doctor.entity';

@Entity({ name: 'slots' })
export class Slot extends AbstractEntity {
  @Column({ name: 'start_hour' }) startHour: number; // start hour of the slot
  @Column({ name: 'start_minute' }) startMinute: number; // start minute of the slot
  @Column({ name: 'end_hour' }) endHour: number; // end hour of the slot
  @Column({ name: 'end_minute' }) endMinute: number; // end minute of the slot

  // equivalent of:
  //   @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
  //   @JoinColumn(name = "id_medecin")
  //   private Medecin medecin;
  //
  // @ManyToOne: several slots for the same doctor.
  // By default, TypeORM does NOT load the [doctor] relation when reading a slot
  // ("lazy" behaviour by default): it must be requested explicitly, through the option
  // `relations: ['doctor']` of a query - exactly as FetchType.LAZY required
  // in JPA an explicit `left join fetch` in the JPQL query to bring the doctor back.
  @ManyToOne(() => Doctor, (doctor) => doctor.slots)
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'doctor_id' })
  doctor: Doctor;

  // equivalent of:
  //   @Column(name = "id_medecin", insertable = false, updatable = false)
  //   private long idMedecin;
  //
  // @RelationId: it is the EXACT and idiomatic TypeORM equivalent of the read-only
  // "idMedecin" field of the original project. It directly exposes the value
  // of the foreign key, WITHOUT having to load the full [Doctor] entity.
  // Very useful to compare identifiers without loading the related entities.
  @RelationId((slot: Slot) => slot.doctor)
  doctorId: number;
}

  • lines 39–41: the many-to-one relationship to the doctor: multiple time slots for one doctor. The foreign key is the [doctor_id] column;

docs.title: 11.8.6. src/entities/appointment.entity.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// entities/appointment.entity.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Equivalent of the JPA entity [Rv] (an appointment):
//
//   @Entity
//   @Table(name = "rv")
//   public class Rv extends AbstractEntity {
//       @Temporal(TemporalType.DATE) private Date jour;
//       @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) @JoinColumn(name = "id_client") private Client client;
//       @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) @JoinColumn(name = "id_creneau") private Creneau creneau;
//       @Column(name = "id_client", insertable = false, updatable = false) private long idClient;
//       @Column(name = "id_creneau", insertable = false, updatable = false) private long idCreneau;
//   }
//
// The SQL uniqueness constraint on (day, slot_id) - which prevents two
// appointments on the same slot on the same day - is defined directly
// in the database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql script (CONSTRAINT unq1_appointments UNIQUE).
// =========================================================================

import { Column, Entity, JoinColumn, ManyToOne, RelationId, Unique } from 'typeorm';
import { AbstractEntity } from './abstract.entity';
import { Client } from './client.entity';
import { Slot } from './slot.entity';

@Entity({ name: 'appointments' })
// recalls, on the TypeORM side, the SQL constraint of the DB script. Beware: we reference here
// the name of the RELATION ('slot'), not the @RelationId field ('slotId') - the latter is
// a "virtual" (computed) column, which TypeORM does not accept in a @Unique constraint.
// TypeORM itself translates 'slot' into its real foreign key column (slot_id).
@Unique('unq1_appointments', ['day', 'slot'])
export class Appointment extends AbstractEntity {
  // equivalent of: @Temporal(TemporalType.DATE) private Date jour;
  // type 'date' (and not 'datetime'): only the day is kept, not the time,
  // exactly as TemporalType.DATE specified on the JPA side.
  @Column({ type: 'date' })
  day: string; // format "yyyy-MM-dd", e.g. "2026-09-13"

  @ManyToOne(() => Client)
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'client_id' })
  client: Client;

  @ManyToOne(() => Slot)
  @JoinColumn({ name: 'slot_id' })
  slot: Slot;

  // equivalents of the read-only idClient / idCreneau fields of the original project
  // (see the detailed explanation in slot.entity.ts about @RelationId)
  @RelationId((appointment: Appointment) => appointment.client)
  clientId: number;

  @RelationId((appointment: Appointment) => appointment.slot)
  slotId: number;
}
  • line 31: an appointment slot is reserved only once per day;
  • lines 36–37: a column of type [DATE], treated as a string [yyyy-mm-dd]: no time zone issues, and two dates are compared as strings;
  • lines 39–45: the client and the appointment time slot;
  • lines 49–53: their IDs.

docs.title: 11.8.7. src/entities/user.entity.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// entities/user.entity.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A user allowed to log in to the application ([users] table).
//
// New in the [dbrdvmedecins2] database: each doctor and each client
// now has THEIR OWN user account ([user] column of the
// [doctors] and [clients] tables, see person.entity.ts). Hence a third role:
//   - ADMIN  : the administrator - appointments + doctor and client management;
//   - DOCTOR : a doctor - books and cancels appointments;
//   - USER   : a client (patient) - books for themselves, manages their account.
//
// Roles remain mutually exclusive: a simple [role] column
// is still enough (no [roles] / [users_roles] table as in the
// original Spring project).
// =========================================================================

import { Column, Entity, Unique } from 'typeorm';
import { AbstractEntity } from './abstract.entity';

export type Role = 'ADMIN' | 'DOCTOR' | 'USER';

@Entity({ name: 'users' })
// a login belongs to one account only (SQL constraint unq_users_login)
@Unique('unq_users_login', ['login'])
export class User extends AbstractEntity {
  @Column({ length: 30 })
  login: string;

  // the HASHED password (bcrypt) - never in clear
  @Column({ length: 100 })
  password: string;

  // the name displayed once logged in - for a doctor or a client:
  // "firstName LASTNAME" (e.g. "Marie PELISSIER")
  @Column({ length: 40 })
  name: string;

  @Column({ type: 'varchar', length: 10 })
  role: Role;
}
  • line 21: a union type of strings: a variable of type [Role] can only be one of these three strings;
  • lines 31–32: the password hash;
  • lines 36–37: the name displayed in the navigation bar (“Marie PELISSIER”);
  • lines 39–40: the role. The column type is specified: [TypeORM] cannot infer a type SQL from a union type.

docs.title: 11.10. The DAO layer
docs.text: One class per table. All follow the model from Example 28: an injected [Repository] [TypeORM], a [repo(manager)] method that selects the repository for the current transaction, and short methods with no business logic.

docs.title: 11.10.1. src/repositories/doctor.repository.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// repositories/doctor.repository.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// DAO layer of the [Doctor] entity. Compared with the JSON server, three
// new features, all related to the management of doctors by the ADMIN:
//   - the reads also bring back the associated user account (relation
//     [user]), to display the login in the list of doctors;
//   - save() / deleteById(): creation, update, deletion;
//   - each write method accepts an OPTIONAL EntityManager: when
//     the business layer provides it, the operation runs INSIDE the transaction
//     of that layer (see business.service.ts, dataSource.transaction(...)).
// =========================================================================

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { EntityManager, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Doctor } from '../entities/doctor.entity';

@Injectable()
export class DoctorRepository {
  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(Doctor)
    private readonly repository: Repository<Doctor>,
  ) {}

  // the Repository to use: the one of the current transaction if there is
  // one, the "ordinary" Repository otherwise.
  private repo(manager?: EntityManager): Repository<Doctor> {
    return manager ? manager.getRepository(Doctor) : this.repository;
  }

  // list sorted by last name then first name, user account included
  findAll(): Promise<Doctor[]> {
    return this.repository.find({ relations: { user: true }, order: { lastName: 'ASC', firstName: 'ASC' } });
  }

  findById(id: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Doctor | null> {
    return this.repo(manager).findOne({ where: { id }, relations: { user: true } });
  }

  // the person with this first and last name, if there is one. The comparison
  // is done by MySQL, hence with the collation of the database (utf8mb4_unicode_ci:
  // regardless of case and accents) - exactly the same
  // rule as the one of the SQL uniqueness constraint.
  findByFirstNameLastName(firstName: string, lastName: string, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Doctor | null> {
    return this.repo(manager).findOneBy({ firstName, lastName });
  }

  save(doctor: Doctor, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Doctor> {
    return this.repo(manager).save(doctor);
  }

  async deleteById(id: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<void> {
    await this.repo(manager).delete(id);
  }
}
  • lines 28–30: within a transaction, the repository for the current transaction ([manager]);
  • lines 33–35: all doctors, along with their account ([relations: { user: true }]), sorted by last name then first name. The account is used to display the login in the list of doctors;
  • lines 45–47: any potential namesakes. The comparison is performed by [MySQL], according to the database’s collation;
  • lines 49–51 and 53–55: write and delete operations.

docs.title: 11.10.2. src/repositories/client.repository.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// repositories/client.repository.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// DAO layer of the [Client] entity (a PATIENT of the practice). Strictly
// the same principle as doctor.repository.ts (see its comments).
// =========================================================================

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { EntityManager, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Client } from '../entities/client.entity';

@Injectable()
export class ClientRepository {
  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(Client)
    private readonly repository: Repository<Client>,
  ) {}

  private repo(manager?: EntityManager): Repository<Client> {
    return manager ? manager.getRepository(Client) : this.repository;
  }

  findAll(): Promise<Client[]> {
    return this.repository.find({ relations: { user: true }, order: { lastName: 'ASC', firstName: 'ASC' } });
  }

  findById(id: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Client | null> {
    return this.repo(manager).findOne({ where: { id }, relations: { user: true } });
  }

  // the client (patient) whose user account is [userId], or null.
  // where: { user: { id } }: TypeORM translates this filter on the relation into
  // a simple "WHERE clients.user = ?" (no join needed)
  findByUserId(userId: number): Promise<Client | null> {
    return this.repository.findOne({ where: { user: { id: userId } }, relations: { user: true } });
  }

  // reads a client while setting a LOCK on its row until the end of the
  // current transaction (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE). A second transaction that
  // requests the same lock WAITS until the first one has finished.
  // Used when booking an appointment (see BusinessService.addAppointment): two
  // simultaneous bookings for the same patient are thus processed one
  // AFTER the other, and the second one sees the appointment created by the first.
  lock(id: number, manager: EntityManager): Promise<Client | null> {
    return manager.getRepository(Client).findOne({ where: { id }, lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' } });
  }

  // the person with this first and last name, if there is one. The comparison
  // is done by MySQL, hence with the collation of the database (utf8mb4_unicode_ci:
  // regardless of case and accents) - exactly the same
  // rule as the one of the SQL uniqueness constraint.
  findByFirstNameLastName(firstName: string, lastName: string, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Client | null> {
    return this.repo(manager).findOneBy({ firstName, lastName });
  }

  save(client: Client, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Client> {
    return this.repo(manager).save(client);
  }

  async deleteById(id: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<void> {
    await this.repo(manager).delete(id);
  }
}

The same methods as for doctors, plus two:

  • lines 35–37: the client whose account is specified—this is how a logged-in patient (whose token contains their account ID) retrieves their client record. [TypeORM] translates the filter [where: { user: { id: userId } }] into [WHERE clients.user = ?];
  • lines 45–47: a read with a lock ([lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' }], i.e., [SELECT ... FOR UPDATE] in SQL). Until the end of the transaction, any other transaction requesting the same lock waits. The appointment scheduling module uses this to process two simultaneous reservations for the same patient one after the other.

// =========================================================================
// repositories/slot.repository.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// DAO layer of the [Slot] entity. New: deleteByDoctor(), used
// when a doctor is deleted (the doctor's time slots disappear
// along with the doctor - see BusinessService.deleteDoctor).
// =========================================================================

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { EntityManager, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Slot } from '../entities/slot.entity';

@Injectable()
export class SlotRepository {
  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(Slot)
    private readonly repository: Repository<Slot>,
  ) {}

  findById(id: number): Promise<Slot | null> {
    return this.repository.findOne({ where: { id }, relations: { doctor: true } });
  }

  // the slots of a doctor, in chronological order
  // (same query as in the JSON server - see its comments)
  getAllSlots(doctorId: number): Promise<Slot[]> {
    return this.repository
      .createQueryBuilder('s')
      .where('s.doctor = :doctorId', { doctorId })
      .orderBy('s.startHour', 'ASC')
      .addOrderBy('s.startMinute', 'ASC')
      .getMany();
  }

  // deletes all the slots of a doctor. delete({ doctor: { id } })
  // generates: DELETE FROM slots WHERE doctor_id = ?
  async deleteByDoctor(doctorId: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<void> {
    const repo = manager ? manager.getRepository(Slot) : this.repository;
    await repo.delete({ doctor: { id: doctorId } });
  }
}
  • Lines 27–34: A doctor’s appointment slots, in chronological order. The query is written using QueryBuilder from [TypeORM], which constructs a SQL query method by method: [createQueryBuilder('s')] (the table, with the alias [s]), [where] (with a parameter named [:doctorId]—never a string concatenation, which would open the door to SQL injections), [orderBy], then [getMany], which executes the query;
  • lines 38–41: Deleting a doctor’s appointment slots, used when that doctor is removed.

docs.title: 11.10.4. src/repositories/appointment.repository.ts
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// repositories/appointment.repository.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// DAO layer of the [Appointment] entity. New features:
//   - the number of appointments of a doctor, to REFUSE the deletion
//     of a doctor who still has appointments (see BusinessService);
//   - the UPCOMING appointments of a client (patient's "My area" page, and
//     rule "only one upcoming appointment per patient");
//   - the deletion of all the appointments of a client (a client is
//     deleted along with their appointments, by the ADMIN or by themselves).
// =========================================================================

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { EntityManager, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Appointment } from '../entities/appointment.entity';

@Injectable()
export class AppointmentRepository {
  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(Appointment)
    private readonly repository: Repository<Appointment>,
  ) {}

  private repo(manager?: EntityManager): Repository<Appointment> {
    return manager ? manager.getRepository(Appointment) : this.repository;
  }

  findById(id: number): Promise<Appointment | null> {
    return this.repository.findOne({ where: { id }, relations: { client: true, slot: true } });
  }

  save(appointment: Appointment, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Appointment> {
    return this.repo(manager).save(appointment);
  }

  async deleteById(id: number): Promise<void> {
    await this.repository.delete(id);
  }

  // the appointments of a doctor on a given day, client and slot included
  // (same query as in the JSON server - see its comments)
  getDoctorDayAppointments(doctorId: number, day: string): Promise<Appointment[]> {
    return this.repository
      .createQueryBuilder('appointment')
      .leftJoinAndSelect('appointment.client', 'client')
      .leftJoinAndSelect('appointment.slot', 'slot')
      .where('slot.doctor = :doctorId', { doctorId })
      .andWhere('appointment.day = :day', { day })
      .getMany();
  }

  // the appointments of a client from day [from] (included), in
  // chronological order, with the slot AND the doctor of that slot
  // (cascading innerJoinAndSelect: appointment -> slot -> doctor)
  findUpcomingByClient(clientId: number, from: string): Promise<Appointment[]> {
    return this.repository
      .createQueryBuilder('appointment')
      .innerJoinAndSelect('appointment.slot', 'slot')
      .innerJoinAndSelect('slot.doctor', 'doctor')
      .where('appointment.client = :clientId', { clientId })
      .andWhere('appointment.day >= :from', { from })
      .orderBy('appointment.day', 'ASC')
      .addOrderBy('slot.startHour', 'ASC')
      .addOrderBy('slot.startMinute', 'ASC')
      .getMany();
  }

  // number of appointments of a client from day [from] (included)
  countUpcomingByClient(clientId: number, from: string, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<number> {
    return this.repo(manager)
      .createQueryBuilder('appointment')
      .where('appointment.client = :clientId', { clientId })
      .andWhere('appointment.day >= :from', { from })
      .getCount();
  }

  // deletes ALL the appointments (past and future) of a client:
  //   DELETE FROM appointments WHERE client_id = ?
  async deleteByClient(clientId: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<void> {
    await this.repo(manager).delete({ client: { id: clientId } });
  }

  // number of appointments (past or future) of a doctor - we must go
  // through the doctor's slots, since [appointments] does not reference [doctors] directly:
  //   SELECT COUNT(*) FROM appointments INNER JOIN slots s ON ... WHERE s.doctor_id = ?
  countByDoctor(doctorId: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<number> {
    return this.repo(manager)
      .createQueryBuilder('appointment')
      .innerJoin('appointment.slot', 'slot')
      .where('slot.doctor = :doctorId', { doctorId })
      .getCount();
  }
}
  • lines 43–51: a doctor’s appointments for a given day. [leftJoinAndSelect] performs a join and loads the joined entity: each appointment is retrieved along with its patient and time slot;
  • lines 56–67: a client’s appointments starting on a given day, with their time slot and the doctor assigned to that slot (two cascading joins): this is what is displayed in “My area”;
  • lines 70–76: their count, for the “only one upcoming appointment” rule;
  • lines 80–82: the deletion of all appointments for a client;
  • lines 87–93: the number of appointments for a doctor. The table [appointments] does not directly reference doctors: you must go through the time slots ([innerJoin], a join without loading).
