docs.title: 5.1.1. The Dictionaries
docs.text:
The file [i18n/fr.json]:

{
  "MENU": {
    "HOME": "Accueil",
    "PRODUCTS": "Produits"
  },
  "HOME": {
    "TITLE": "Bienvenue",
    "HELLO": "Bonjour {name} !",
    "DATE": "Nous sommes le {date}."
  },
  "PRODUCTS": {
    "TITLE": "Nos produits",
    "NAME": "Produit",
    "PRICE": "Prix",
    "COUNT": "{n} produit(s) au catalogue."
  }
}

The file [i18n/en.json]:

{
  "MENU": {
    "HOME": "Home",
    "PRODUCTS": "Products"
  },
  "HOME": {
    "TITLE": "Welcome",
    "HELLO": "Hello {name}!",
    "DATE": "Today is {date}."
  },
  "PRODUCTS": {
    "TITLE": "Our products",
    "NAME": "Product",
    "PRICE": "Price",
    "COUNT": "{n} product(s) in the catalogue."
  }
}
  • A dictionary is a JSON file, organized by page or by topic: The key [HOME.HELLO] refers to the text [HELLO] in section [HOME];
  • Line 8: A text may contain parameters, enclosed in curly braces, which are replaced during translation. Word order varies from one language to another: this is why a text is not created by simply concatenating translated segments.

docs.title: 5.1.2. The translation module
docs.text:
The file [src/i18n.ts]:

import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import { join } from 'path';

export type Language = 'fr' | 'en';
export const LANGUAGES: Language[] = ['fr', 'en'];
export const DEFAULT_LANGUAGE: Language = 'en';
// the "locale" used by Intl for dates and numbers
export const LOCALES: Record<Language, string> = { fr: 'fr-FR', en: 'en-US' };

// a dictionary is a nested JSON object: { "MENU": { "HOME": "Home" } }
type Dictionary = { [key: string]: string | Dictionary };

// the dictionaries are read ONCE, at startup
const FOLDER = join(__dirname, '..', 'i18n');
const dictionaries: Record<Language, Dictionary> = {
  fr: JSON.parse(readFileSync(join(FOLDER, 'fr.json'), 'utf-8')),
  en: JSON.parse(readFileSync(join(FOLDER, 'en.json'), 'utf-8')),
};

export function isLanguage(value: unknown): value is Language {
  return typeof value === 'string' && (LANGUAGES as string[]).includes(value);
}

// translate('en', 'HOME.HELLO', { name: 'Marie' }) -> "Hello Marie!"
export function translate(language: Language, key: string, params: Record<string, unknown> = {}): string {
  const text = lookup(dictionaries[language], key) ?? key;
  return text.replace(/\{(\w+)\}/g, (whole, name: string) => (name in params ? String(params[name]) : whole));
}

// 'HOME.HELLO': we go down into HOME, then into HELLO
function lookup(dictionary: Dictionary, key: string): string | null {
  let node: string | Dictionary | undefined = dictionary;
  for (const part of key.split('.')) {
    if (typeof node !== 'object') {
      return null;
    }
    node = node[part];
  }
  return typeof node === 'string' ? node : null;
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 4–6: the supported languages;
  • line 8: the “locale” for each language, used by [Intl] to format dates and numbers ([fr-FR]: 23/09/2026, 12,50 €; [en-US]: 9/23/2026, €12.50);
  • lines 14–18: the dictionaries are read once, when the module loads, and then kept in memory;
  • lines 20–22: a check for a type such as [TypeScript] ([value is Language]): after a positive test, the compiler knows that the value is a [Language];
  • lines 25–28: the translation. The key is looked up in the dictionary; if it is not found, the key itself is displayed: any omission is immediately visible on the screen. The regular expression [/\{(\w+)\}/g] finds each parameter [{name}] and replaces it with its value;
  • lines 31–40: The key [HOME.HELLO] is split into [HOME] and then [HELLO], and the process continues down into the object JSON.

docs.title: 5.1.3. The helpers
docs.text:
The file [src/helpers.ts]:

import { HelperOptions } from 'handlebars';
import { Language, DEFAULT_LANGUAGE, LOCALES, isLanguage, translate } from './i18n';

interface Hbs {
  registerHelper(name: string, fn: (...args: any[]) => unknown): void;
}

// the language of the page: res.locals.lang, merged into the root model
function languageOf(options: HelperOptions): Language {
  const lang = options.data?.root?.lang;
  return isLanguage(lang) ? lang : DEFAULT_LANGUAGE;
}

export function registerHelpers(hbs: Hbs): void {
  // {{t 'KEY'}} or {{t 'KEY' name=...}}: translation, with named parameters
  hbs.registerHelper('t', (key: string, options: HelperOptions) => translate(languageOf(options), key, options.hash));

  // {{longDate when}}: "mercredi 23 septembre 2026" / "Wednesday, September 23, 2026"
  hbs.registerHelper('longDate', (when: string, options: HelperOptions) =>
    new Intl.DateTimeFormat(LOCALES[languageOf(options)], { dateStyle: 'full' }).format(new Date(when)),
  );

  // {{money price}}: "12,50 €" / "€12.50"
  hbs.registerHelper('money', (amount: number, options: HelperOptions) =>
    new Intl.NumberFormat(LOCALES[languageOf(options)], { style: 'currency', currency: 'EUR' }).format(amount),
  );

  hbs.registerHelper('eq', (a: unknown, b: unknown) => a === b);
}
  • lines 9–12: The page’s language is in the root template ([options.data.root.lang]), where the [main.ts] middleware placed it via [res.locals];
  • line 16: the helper [t] translates a key. The named parameters of the helper ([options.hash]) are the text parameters: [{{t 'HOME.HELLO' name=name}}];
  • lines 19–21 and 24–26: dates and amounts are formatted according to the language.

docs.title: 5.1.4. Language Selection
docs.text:
The file [src/main.ts]:

import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { NestExpressApplication } from '@nestjs/platform-express';
import * as cookieParser from 'cookie-parser';
import { NextFunction, Request, Response } from 'express';
import * as hbs from 'hbs';
import { dirname, join } from 'path';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';
import { registerHelpers } from './helpers';
import { isLanguage, DEFAULT_LANGUAGE } from './i18n';

const ROOT = join(__dirname, '..');

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create<NestExpressApplication>(AppModule);
  app.useStaticAssets(join(dirname(require.resolve('bootstrap/package.json')), 'dist'), { prefix: '/bootstrap/' });
  app.setBaseViewsDir(join(ROOT, 'views'));
  app.setViewEngine('hbs');
  registerHelpers(hbs);
  await new Promise<void>((done) => hbs.registerPartials(join(ROOT, 'views', 'partials'), () => done()));
  app.use(cookieParser());
  // the language of each page: that of the [language] cookie, English otherwise
  app.use((req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) => {
    const cookie = req.cookies?.language;
    res.locals.lang = isLanguage(cookie) ? cookie : DEFAULT_LANGUAGE;
    next();
  });
  await app.listen(3000);
  console.log('Server started on http://localhost:3000');
}

bootstrap();

Lines 22–26: For each request, the language is read from the [language] cookie (English by default) and stored in [res.locals.lang], and thus in the template for each view.

The file [src/language.controller.ts]:

import { Controller, Get, NotFoundException, Param, Req, Res } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Request, Response } from 'express';
import { isLanguage } from './i18n';

@Controller('language')
export class LanguageController {
  // GET /language/fr: stores the choice in a cookie, then goes back to the previous page
  @Get(':language')
  change(@Param('language') language: string, @Req() req: Request, @Res() res: Response): void {
    if (!isLanguage(language)) {
      throw new NotFoundException();
    }
    res.cookie('language', language, { maxAge: 365 * 24 * 3600 * 1000, sameSite: 'lax', httpOnly: true });
    res.redirect(originPage(req));
  }
}

// the page we come from (Referer header), of which we keep only the path:
// redirecting to a full address taken from the request would allow
// sending the user to another site ("open redirect" vulnerability)
function originPage(req: Request): string {
  const referer = req.get('referer');
  if (!referer) {
    return '/';
  }
  try {
    const url = new URL(referer);
    return url.pathname + url.search;
  } catch {
    return '/';
  }
}
  • lines 8–15: [GET /language/en] stores the selection in a cookie valid for one year, then redirects to the page the user came from. An unknown language results in a 404 error;
  • lines 21–32: The original page is specified by the [Referer] header, which the browser adds when a link is clicked. We retain only the path: redirecting to a full URL from the request would allow a malicious site to create a link that, after passing through our site, sends the user to the malicious site (a vulnerability known as [open redirect]).

docs.text:
The [views/layout.hbs] file:

The [src/pages.controller.ts] file:

import { Controller, Get, Render } from '@nestjs/common';

@Controller()
export class PagesController {
  @Get()
  @Render('home')
  home(): object {
    // pageTitle is a KEY: the view translates it
    return { pageTitle: 'HOME.TITLE', name: 'Marie', today: '2026-09-23' };
  }

  @Get('products')
  @Render('products')
  products(): object {
    const products = [
      { name: 'Keyboard', price: 25 },
      { name: 'Mouse', price: 12.5 },
      { name: 'Screen', price: 1149 },
    ];
    return { pageTitle: 'PRODUCTS.TITLE', products, count: products.length };
  }
}

docs.text:

Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 31

Found. Redirecting to /products

The server sets the cookie and redirects to the original page, which is now in English:

The case study proceeds exactly this way, using more comprehensive dictionaries ([i18n/fr.json] and [i18n/en.json]): same helper [t], same controller [/language/:language], same cookie. There is only one difference: the error messages generated by the business and web layers are also keys, translated at the last moment by the view.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The document’s PDF is |HERE|.

The document’s codes are |HERE|.

This document is a product of Anthropic’s IA Claude. Its purpose is to adapt the document *Introduction to ASP.NET MVC by Example* (2013) to the [NestJS] web framework:

  • the [ASP.NET MVC] framework and the [C#] language are replaced by the [NestJS] framework and the [TypeScript] language;
  • the [Razor] views are replaced by [Handlebars] views;
  • [Entity Framework] data access is replaced by ORM, [TypeORM], and a [MySQL] database.

The document follows the structure of the original course: first, numerous small projects, each focused on a single concept, followed by a comprehensive case study—a web application for scheduling appointments at a medical practice—with all files fully commented. The chapter from the original course devoted to the basics of web programming (the HTTP protocol, the HTML language) has not been included: these basics are assumed to be known.

docs.title: 1.1. The Role of NestJS in a Web Application
docs.text:
A web application is often built in layers, with each layer communicating only with its neighboring layers:

  • the web layer receives HTTP requests from the browser and returns HTML pages to it. [NestJS] helps us write this layer;
  • the business layer contains the application’s business rules (e.g., “a patient can have only one upcoming appointment”). It knows nothing about the web: it could just as easily serve a command-line application;
  • the data access layer (layer [DAO], for [Data Access Object]) reads from and writes to the database. We will use the ORM [TypeORM] ([Object Relational Mapper]), which maps the rows of the tables to the [TypeScript] objects.

The web layer itself follows the [MVC] ([Model – View – Controller]) model:

  • the controller (C) is a class whose methods—called actions—each handle a specific type of request (for example, [GET /schedule]). An action reads the request parameters, invokes the business layer, and then selects the view to display;
  • the model (M) is the set of data that the action passes to the view: a simple [JavaScript] object;
  • the view (V) is a [Handlebars] file (extension [.hbs]): a HTML file in which [{{...}}] tags are replaced by data from the model.

The processing of a request follows the numbered steps in the diagram:

  • 1: The browser sends a HTTP request, for example, [GET /schedule?doctorId=1&day=2026-09-24];
  • 2: [NestJS], which relies on the web server [Express], selects the action responsible for handling this request: this is routing. Before reaching that point, the request may pass through middleware, guards, interceptors, and pipes, which we’ll explore in the following chapters;
  • 3: The action requests the data it needs from the business layer;
  • 4: It builds the view template and specifies the view that should display it;
  • 5: The [Handlebars] view engine generates the HTML page, which [NestJS] returns to the browser.

[NestJS] is a [Node.js] framework written in [TypeScript]. It builds on the concepts of the [Spring] ([Java]) and [Angular] frameworks: decorators ([@Controller], [@Get], [@Injectable]...) describe the role of each class, and dependency injection provides each object with the dependencies it needs. It is often used to write servers that return JSON to a client [JavaScript] ([Angular], [React], [Flutter]...). This document uses it to write a classic web application: the server generates the HTML pages, and the browser simply displays them.

docs.title: 1.2. Tools Used
docs.text:
The examples were written and tested using the following tools (their installation is described in the appendix):

  • [Node.js] 20 and its package manager [npm];
  • the editor [Visual Studio Code];
  • a recent browser ([Chrome], [Firefox], [Edge]);
  • the command-line tool [curl], which displays raw HTTP responses (it is included with [Windows] 10 and 11);
  • the SGBD [MySQL] (or [MariaDB]), for example, the one for [Laragon] under [Windows], starting with the chapter on data access.

The library versions are those in the [package.json] file in the examples folder: [NestJS] 10, [TypeScript] 5, [hbs] 4 ([Handlebars]), [class-validator] 0.14, [TypeORM] 0.3, [Bootstrap] 5.

docs.title: 1.3. Examples
docs.text:
The examples are stored in a folder named [examples], with one subfolder per example:

examples/
├── 01-structure/
├── 02-routing/
├── ...
├── 28-layers/
├── node_modules/
├── package.json
└── package-lock.json

All examples share the same libraries, which are declared in [examples/package.json]. They are installed once, in a console opened to the [examples] folder. In VSCode, open the examples folder:

then, in a terminal integrated into VSCode, type the command

npm install

Each example then has the minimal structure of a [NestJS] project:

13-first-view/
├── src/
│   ├── app.module.ts
│   ├── main.ts
│   └── views.controller.ts
├── views/
│   ├── index.hbs
│   └── unknown.hbs
├── nest-cli.json
└── tsconfig.json
  • [src]: the code [TypeScript];
  • [views]: the views from [Handlebars] (starting in Chapter 4);
  • [nest-cli.json]: the command-line tool configuration for [NestJS];
  • [tsconfig.json]: the configuration of the [TypeScript] compiler.

To run an example, open a console in the

and type:

npx nest start

[npx] locates the tool [nest] in the [node_modules] folder within the parent folder. [nest start] compiles the code [TypeScript] in the [dist] folder, then executes [dist/main.js]. With the [--watch] option, the code is recompiled and the server restarted whenever a [.ts] file is modified:

npx nest start --watch

All examples listen on port 3000: only one can be running at a time. Stop the server using [Ctrl-C] in the console.

The file [tsconfig.json] is the same for all examples:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "commonjs",
    "target": "ES2022",
    "lib": ["ES2022"],
    "outDir": "./dist",
    "rootDir": "./src",
    "sourceMap": true,
    "emitDecoratorMetadata": true,
    "experimentalDecorators": true,
    "allowSyntheticDefaultImports": true,
    "strictNullChecks": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}

Let’s comment on this file:

  • line 3: the compiled code uses the modules [CommonJS] from [Node.js] ([require]);
  • line 4: the generated code is from the recent [JavaScript] (ES2022), which includes [Node.js] 20;
  • lines 6–7: the source code is in [src], and the compiled code is in [dist];
  • lines 9–10: required for [NestJS]. Decorators ([@Controller]...) are a feature of [TypeScript] that must be enabled, and [emitDecoratorMetadata] preserves the types of constructor and method parameters in the compiled code: it is thanks to this that [NestJS] knows which object to inject into a constructor;
  • Line 12: The compiler reports the use of a value that may be [null] or [undefined];
  • line 13: library declaration files are not checked (faster compilation).

The file [nest-cli.json] is also common to all examples:

{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/nest-cli",
  "collection": "@nestjs/schematics",
  "sourceRoot": "src",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "deleteOutDir": true
  }
}
  • line 4: the source code is in [src];
  • line 6: the [dist] folder is emptied before each compilation (a file deleted from [src] does not leave behind an outdated compiled copy).

docs.title: 9. Layered Architecture and Data Access
docs.text:
The previous examples kept their data in memory. A real application stores it in a database and is organized into layers (see the diagram in the introduction):

  • the web layer (controllers, views): read the request, call the business layer, select the view;
  • the business layer: business rules;
  • the DAO layer: database queries.

Each layer is aware only of the layer below it, and as few details about it as possible: the web layer is unaware of the SQL layer, and the business layer is unaware of the HTML layer. This separation makes each layer easier to understand, test, and evolve. Example 28 applies this to managing a list of people: it is, on a smaller scale, the management of doctors and clients from the case study.

docs.title: 9.1.1. The database
docs.text:
The database [dbpersons] is created by a script SQL. Using [Laragon], it can be run, for example, in the [HeidiSQL] tool (File menu / Run a SQL file), or from the command line:

mysql -u root < database/dbpersons.sql

The [database/dbpersons.sql] file:

-- database of example 28: a single table, [persons]
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS dbpersons;
CREATE DATABASE dbpersons CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbpersons;

CREATE TABLE persons (
  id INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  first_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  last_name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  age INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (id),
  -- two persons cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_persons_first_name_last_name UNIQUE (first_name, last_name)
) ENGINE = InnoDB;

INSERT INTO persons (first_name, last_name, age) VALUES
  ('Marie', 'Pélissier', 42),
  ('Jacques', 'Bromard', 35),
  ('Philippe', 'Jandot', 58);
  • Line 3: The [utf8mb4] character set accepts all characters (accents, emojis, etc.). The collation [utf8mb4_unicode_ci] compares strings without regard to uppercase letters or accents: for MySQL, [pelissier], and [Pélissier] are equal;
  • line 8: a version number, incremented each time the line is modified (see “optimistic lock,” below);
  • line 14: a named uniqueness constraint: the database does not allow two people with the same first and last names. The name will be used to identify the error.

docs.title: 9.1.2. The configuration of TypeORM
docs.text:
The [src/config/database.config.ts] file:

import { TypeOrmModuleOptions } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Person } from '../entities/person.entity';

// the database connection; the default values are those of Laragon
export function databaseConfig(): TypeOrmModuleOptions {
  return {
    type: 'mysql',
    host: process.env.DB_HOST ?? 'localhost',
    port: Number(process.env.DB_PORT ?? 3306),
    username: process.env.DB_USERNAME ?? 'root',
    password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD ?? '',
    database: 'dbpersons',
    entities: [Person],
    // the schema is created by the SQL script, never modified by TypeORM
    synchronize: false,
    // DB_LOGGING=true: displays the SQL statements sent to the database
    logging: process.env.DB_LOGGING === 'true',
  };
}
  • Lines 8–11: connection parameters, read from environment variables, with the default values from [Laragon] (username [root], no password);
  • line 13: the classes that [TypeORM] maps to tables;
  • line 15: [TypeORM] could create or modify the tables itself based on the classes. This is convenient for a prototype but dangerous for a database containing data: the schema remains the responsibility of the SQL script;
  • line 17: with the environment variable [DB_LOGGING=true], the SQL commands sent to the database are displayed in the console.

docs.title: 9.1.3. The Person entity
docs.text:
The file [src/entities/person.entity.ts]:

import { Column, Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, VersionColumn } from 'typeorm';

// a row of the [persons] table <-> a Person object
@Entity('persons')
export class Person {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn()
  id: number;

  // incremented by TypeORM on each modification (optimistic lock)
  @VersionColumn()
  version: number;

  @Column({ name: 'first_name', length: 30 })
  firstName: string;

  @Column({ name: 'last_name', length: 30 })
  lastName: string;

  @Column()
  age: number;
}
  • Line 4: The class [Person] corresponds to the table [persons]: each row of the table will be a [Person] object;
  • line 6: the primary key, generated by the database ([AUTO_INCREMENT]);
  • Line 10: the version column, managed by [TypeORM];
  • rows 13–20: the other columns.

docs.title: 9.1.4. The DAO layer
docs.text:
The file [src/dao/persons.dao.ts]:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { EntityManager, Not, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Person } from '../entities/person.entity';

// the DATA ACCESS layer: queries, no business rules
@Injectable()
export class PersonsDao {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Person) private readonly repository: Repository<Person>) {}

  // inside a transaction, we must go through the transaction's "manager"
  private repo(manager?: EntityManager): Repository<Person> {
    return manager ? manager.getRepository(Person) : this.repository;
  }

  list(): Promise<Person[]> {
    return this.repository.find({ order: { lastName: 'ASC', firstName: 'ASC' } });
  }

  read(id: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Person | null> {
    return this.repo(manager).findOneBy({ id });
  }

  // ANOTHER person (id different from [exceptId]) with these first and last names
  namesake(firstName: string, lastName: string, exceptId: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Person | null> {
    return this.repo(manager).findOneBy({ firstName, lastName, id: Not(exceptId) });
  }

  // INSERT if the person has no id, UPDATE otherwise
  save(person: Person, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<Person> {
    return this.repo(manager).save(person);
  }

  async delete(id: number, manager?: EntityManager): Promise<void> {
    await this.repo(manager).delete(id);
  }
}
  • line 9: [TypeORM] provides a repository ([Repository<Person>]) for each entity that can read from and write to the table. [@InjectRepository] injects it;
  • lines 12–14: Within a transaction, all queries must go through the same [EntityManager] object—the one associated with the transaction. Each method therefore accepts an optional [manager];
  • lines 16–18: [find] with a sort: [SELECT ... ORDER BY last_name, first_name];
  • lines 25–27: a person with the same first and last name, other than [exceptId] ([Not]): useful for modifying a record, which must not conflict with itself;
  • lines 30–32: [save] becomes [INSERT] if the object has no identifier, and [UPDATE] otherwise.

The DAO layer contains no rules: only queries.

docs.title: 9.1.5. The business layer
docs.text:
The file [src/business/business.exception.ts]:

// a business rule rejects the operation: this is not an anomaly,
// the message is intended for the user
export class BusinessException extends Error {}

A [BusinessException] indicates that a business rule has rejected an operation. This is not a program error: the message is intended for the user.

The [src/business/persons.business.ts] file:

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource, EntityManager } from 'typeorm';
import { PersonsDao } from '../dao/persons.dao';
import { Person } from '../entities/person.entity';
import { BusinessException } from './business.exception';

export interface PersonData {
  firstName: string;
  lastName: string;
  age: number;
}

// the BUSINESS layer: the business rules, and only them
@Injectable()
export class PersonsBusiness {
  constructor(
    private readonly dao: PersonsDao,
    private readonly dataSource: DataSource,
  ) {}

  list(): Promise<Person[]> {
    return this.dao.list();
  }

  async read(id: number): Promise<Person> {
    const person = await this.dao.read(id);
    if (!person) {
      throw new BusinessException('This person does not exist (anymore).');
    }
    return person;
  }

  add(data: PersonData): Promise<Person> {
    return this.transaction(async (manager) => {
      // rule 1: no two persons with the same first and last names
      if (await this.dao.namesake(data.firstName, data.lastName, 0, manager)) {
        throw new BusinessException('A person already has these first and last names.');
      }
      const person = new Person();
      person.firstName = data.firstName;
      person.lastName = data.lastName;
      person.age = data.age;
      return this.dao.save(person, manager);
    });
  }

  edit(id: number, version: number, data: PersonData): Promise<Person> {
    return this.transaction(async (manager) => {
      const person = await this.dao.read(id, manager);
      if (!person) {
        throw new BusinessException('This person does not exist (anymore).');
      }
      // rule 2: we do not modify a record modified meanwhile by someone else
      if (person.version !== version) {
        throw new BusinessException('This record has been modified meanwhile: reload it.');
      }
      if (await this.dao.namesake(data.firstName, data.lastName, id, manager)) {
        throw new BusinessException('A person already has these first and last names.');
      }
      person.firstName = data.firstName;
      person.lastName = data.lastName;
      person.age = data.age;
      return this.dao.save(person, manager);
    });
  }

  async delete(id: number): Promise<Person> {
    const person = await this.read(id);
    await this.dao.delete(id);
    return person;
  }

  // [work] runs inside a transaction: COMMIT if it succeeds, ROLLBACK
  // if it throws an exception. A violation of the uniqueness constraint (two
  // simultaneous additions, for example) becomes a BusinessException
  private async transaction<R>(work: (manager: EntityManager) => Promise<R>): Promise<R> {
    try {
      return await this.dataSource.transaction(work);
    } catch (e) {
      const sqlError = e as { code?: string; message?: string };
      if (sqlError.code === 'ER_DUP_ENTRY' && sqlError.message?.includes('unq_persons_first_name_last_name')) {
        throw new BusinessException('A person already has these first and last names.');
      }
      throw e;
    }
  }
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • lines 16–19: The business layer uses DAO, and [DataSource] from [TypeORM] (the database connection) to open transactions;
  • lines 25–31: an absent person is a [BusinessException];
  • lines 33–45: adding a person within a transaction. Rule: no two people may have the same first and last names. This is verified before the write operation to display a clear message;
  • lines 47–65: modification. Additional rule: the optimistic lock (lines 54–56): the modification form carries the version of the record as it was when the form was opened. If it has changed in the meantime (another user has modified the same record), the operation is rejected rather than silently overwriting the user’s work;
  • lines 76–86: [dataSource.transaction(work)] opens a transaction, executes [work], then validates it ([COMMIT]) or rolls it back ([ROLLBACK]) if [work] throws an exception. Lines 81–82: Preliminary checking for homonyms is not always sufficient: two users may add the same person at the same time, and both may pass the check. The database’s uniqueness constraint, however, does not allow any exceptions; the error MySQL [ER_DUP_ENTRY], identified by the constraint, then becomes the same [BusinessException].

docs.title: 9.1.6. The Web Layer
docs.text:
The file [src/web/person-form.dto.ts]:

import { Transform, Type } from 'class-transformer';
import { IsInt, IsNotEmpty, Max, MaxLength, Min } from 'class-validator';

const clean = ({ value }: { value: unknown }) => (typeof value === 'string' ? value.trim() : value);

// the fields of the form and their constraints (lengths = SQL columns)
export class PersonFormDto {
  @Transform(clean)
  @IsNotEmpty({ message: 'The first name is required.' })
  @MaxLength(30, { message: 'The first name must not exceed 30 characters.' })
  firstName: string;

  @Transform(clean)
  @IsNotEmpty({ message: 'The last name is required.' })
  @MaxLength(30, { message: 'The last name must not exceed 30 characters.' })
  lastName: string;

  @Type(() => Number)
  @IsInt({ message: 'The age must be an integer.' })
  @Min(0, { message: 'The age must be positive.' })
  @Max(150, { message: 'The age cannot exceed 150.' })
  age: number;
}

The form and its constraints (see Example 19). The function [validateForm] (file [web/validation.ts]) is the one from Example 19, and [web/flash.ts] is the one from Example 20, supplemented with a message type (success or error).

The file [src/web/persons.controller.ts]:

import { Body, Controller, Get, Param, ParseIntPipe, Post, Redirect, Render, Res } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Response } from 'express';
import { BusinessException } from '../business/business.exception';
import { PersonsBusiness } from '../business/persons.business';
import { flash } from './flash';
import { PersonFormDto } from './person-form.dto';
import { validateForm } from './validation';

// the WEB layer: read the request, call the business layer, choose the view
@Controller()
export class PersonsController {
  constructor(private readonly business: PersonsBusiness) {}

  @Get()
  @Redirect('/persons')
  root(): void {}

  @Get('persons')
  @Render('list')
  async list(): Promise<object> {
    return { persons: await this.business.list() };
  }

  @Get('persons/add')
  @Render('form')
  addForm(): object {
    return { title: 'Add a person', action: '/persons/add', values: {}, errors: {} };
  }

  @Post('persons/add')
  async add(@Body() body: Record<string, string>, @Res() res: Response): Promise<void> {
    const view = { title: 'Add a person', action: '/persons/add' };
    const { dto, errors } = await validateForm(PersonFormDto, body);
    if (Object.keys(errors).length > 0) {
      res.render('form', { ...view, values: body, errors, error: 'The form contains errors.' });
      return;
    }
    try {
      const p = await this.business.add(dto);
      flash(res, { type: 'success', text: `${p.firstName} ${p.lastName} has been added.` });
      res.redirect('/persons');
    } catch (e) {
      // a business rule rejected the addition: we display the form again
      if (!(e instanceof BusinessException)) throw e;
      res.render('form', { ...view, values: body, errors: {}, error: e.message });
    }
  }

  @Get('persons/:id/edit')
  @Render('form')
  async editForm(@Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number): Promise<object> {
    const p = await this.business.read(id);
    return { title: 'Edit a person', action: `/persons/${id}/edit`, values: p, errors: {} };
  }

  @Post('persons/:id/edit')
  async edit(
    @Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number,
    @Body() body: Record<string, string>,
    @Res() res: Response,
  ): Promise<void> {
    const view = { title: 'Edit a person', action: `/persons/${id}/edit` };
    const { dto, errors } = await validateForm(PersonFormDto, body);
    if (Object.keys(errors).length > 0) {
      res.render('form', { ...view, values: body, errors, error: 'The form contains errors.' });
      return;
    }
    try {
      const p = await this.business.edit(id, Number(body.version), dto);
      flash(res, { type: 'success', text: `${p.firstName} ${p.lastName} has been modified.` });
      res.redirect('/persons');
    } catch (e) {
      if (!(e instanceof BusinessException)) throw e;
      res.render('form', { ...view, values: body, errors: {}, error: e.message });
    }
  }

  @Post('persons/:id/delete')
  async delete(@Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number, @Res() res: Response): Promise<void> {
    try {
      const p = await this.business.delete(id);
      flash(res, { type: 'success', text: `${p.firstName} ${p.lastName} has been deleted.` });
    } catch (e) {
      if (!(e instanceof BusinessException)) throw e;
      // no form to display again: the error travels as a flash too
      flash(res, { type: 'danger', text: e.message });
    }
    res.redirect('/persons');
  }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 12: the controller only knows the business layer;
  • lines 14–16: the site root redirects to the list;
  • lines 18–22: an asynchronous action: the list is retrieved from the database;
  • lines 30–47: the addition, in three steps: form validation (errors → page reload), call to the business layer (success → pop-up message and redirection), [BusinessException] (→ page reload with the message at the bottom of the page). Another exception is thrown ([throw e]): this is an anomaly, which the exception filter for [NestJS] will convert into a 500 error;
  • lines 49–54: the update form, pre-filled with the record retrieved from the database (including its version);
  • lines 56–61: same process as for adding a record; the version returned by the form is passed to the business layer;
  • lines 78–89: deletion. There is no form to redisplay: any errors are also included in the flash message.

The file [src/app.module.ts]:

import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { TypeOrmModule } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { databaseConfig } from './config/database.config';
import { PersonsDao } from './dao/persons.dao';
import { Person } from './entities/person.entity';
import { PersonsBusiness } from './business/persons.business';
import { PersonsController } from './web/persons.controller';

@Module({
  imports: [
    // the database connection, for the whole application
    TypeOrmModule.forRoot(databaseConfig()),
    // the Repository<T> injectable in this module
    TypeOrmModule.forFeature([Person]),
  ],
  controllers: [PersonsController],
  // the three layers: web (controller) -> business -> dao
  providers: [PersonsBusiness, PersonsDao],
})
export class AppModule {}
  • line 12: the database connection for the entire application;
  • line 14: enables the [Repository<Person>] to be injected;
  • line 18: the business layer services and DAO.

The [views/form.hbs] file:

<h1 class="h3">{{title}}</h1>
<form method="post" action="{{action}}" novalidate>
  {{!-- the version of the record read, sent back with the modification --}}
  <input type="hidden" name="version" value="{{values.version}}">
  <div class="row g-2 mb-3">
    <div class="col-sm-5">
      <label class="form-label" for="firstName">First name</label>
      <input class="form-control {{#if errors.firstName}}is-invalid{{/if}}" id="firstName" name="firstName"
             value="{{values.firstName}}" maxlength="30" required>
      {{#if errors.firstName}}<div class="invalid-feedback">{{errors.firstName}}</div>{{/if}}
    </div>
    <div class="col-sm-5">
      <label class="form-label" for="lastName">Last name</label>
      <input class="form-control {{#if errors.lastName}}is-invalid{{/if}}" id="lastName" name="lastName"
             value="{{values.lastName}}" maxlength="30" required>
      {{#if errors.lastName}}<div class="invalid-feedback">{{errors.lastName}}</div>{{/if}}
    </div>
    <div class="col-sm-2">
      <label class="form-label" for="age">Age</label>
      <input class="form-control {{#if errors.age}}is-invalid{{/if}}" id="age" name="age" type="number"
             value="{{values.age}}" required>
      {{#if errors.age}}<div class="invalid-feedback">{{errors.age}}</div>{{/if}}
    </div>
  </div>
  <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Save</button>
  <a class="btn btn-link" href="/persons">Back to the list</a>
</form>

Line 4: the hidden field that carries the record’s version. The view is used for adding and modifying records: its title and the submission URL ([action]) are provided by the controller. The views [list.hbs] and [layout.hbs], along with the confirmation script, are the same as those in Examples 20 and 21.

docs.title: 9.1.7. Execution
docs.text:
Connection parameters are passed via environment variables if the default values are not suitable. Under [Windows] ([PowerShell]):

$env:DB_USERNAME="root"; $env:DB_PASSWORD=""; $env:DB_LOGGING="true"; npx nest start

The list:

An invalid form:

A homonym, written in lowercase and without accents: the business rule detects it, because MySQL compares based on the database's collation:

A successful addition, and the corresponding SQL orders ([DB_LOGGING=true]):

query: START TRANSACTION
query: SELECT `Person`.`id` AS `Person_id`, `Person`.`version` AS `Person_version`, `Person`.`first_name` AS `Person_first_name`, `Person`.`last_name` AS `Person_last_name`, `Person`.`age` AS `Person_age` FROM `persons` `Person` WHERE ((`Person`.`first_name` = ?) AND (`Person`.`last_name` = ?) AND (`Person`.`id` != ?)) LIMIT 1 -- PARAMETERS: ["Sylvie","Durand",0]
query: INSERT INTO `persons`(`id`, `version`, `first_name`, `last_name`, `age`) VALUES (DEFAULT, 1, ?, ?, ?) -- PARAMETERS: ["Sylvie","Durand",29]
query: SELECT `Person`.`id` AS `Person_id`, `Person`.`version` AS `Person_version` FROM `persons` `Person` WHERE `Person`.`id` = ? -- PARAMETERS: [4]
query: COMMIT
query: SELECT `Person`.`id` AS `Person_id`, `Person`.`version` AS `Person_version`, `Person`.`first_name` AS `Person_first_name`, `Person`.`last_name` AS `Person_last_name`, `Person`.`age` AS `Person_age` FROM `persons` `Person` ORDER BY `Person`.`last_name` ASC, `Person`.`first_name` ASC

We can see the transaction ([START TRANSACTION] ... [COMMIT]), the search for duplicates, the insertion with version 1, and then, after the redirection, the reading of the list. The optimistic lock: two forms are open on the same record; the first is saved (the version changes to 2); the second, which still has version 1, is rejected:

Deletion, with confirmation:

docs.title: 3. The Action Model
docs.text: An action requires information sent by the browser: the URL parameters ([?name=martin&age=42]), form fields, and route parameters. The original course refers to all of this information as the action’s model. This chapter shows how [NestJS] provides it to the action, converts it to the correct type, and validates it.

docs.title: 3.1. Example 07: URL Parameters
docs.text:
The [src/parameters.controller.ts] file:

import { Controller, DefaultValuePipe, Get, ParseIntPipe, Query } from '@nestjs/common';

@Controller('parameters')
export class ParametersController {
  // /parameters/action01?name=martin
  @Get('action01')
  action01(@Query('name') name: string): string {
    return `name = [${name}], of type ${typeof name}`;
  }

  // /parameters/action02?age=42: a parameter is ALWAYS a string
  @Get('action02')
  action02(@Query('age') age: number): string {
    return `age = [${age}], of type ${typeof age}`;
  }

  // /parameters/action03?age=42: ParseIntPipe converts (or rejects)
  @Get('action03')
  action03(@Query('age', ParseIntPipe) age: number): string {
    return `age = [${age}], of type ${typeof age}`;
  }

  // /parameters/action04?page=2: a default value if the parameter is missing
  @Get('action04')
  action04(@Query('page', new DefaultValuePipe(1), ParseIntPipe) page: number): string {
    return `page = [${page}], of type ${typeof page}`;
  }

  // /parameters/action05?name=martin&age=42: all the parameters at once
  @Get('action05')
  action05(@Query() parameters: Record<string, string>): object {
    return parameters;
  }
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • Lines 6–9: [@Query('name')] inserts the value of the [name] parameter from URL (the part following [?], called the query string or [query string]);
  • lines 12–15: the parameter [age] is declared as type [number]... but this type is merely a declaration [TypeScript], which is removed at compile time. What we receive is always a string, as shown by the execution;
  • lines 18–21: [ParseIntPipe] is a pipe: an object that transforms (and validates) a parameter’s value before it reaches the action. Here, the string ['42'] becomes the number 42; a non-numeric string causes a 400 (Bad Request) error, without the action being executed;
  • lines 24–27: the pipes are chained together: [DefaultValuePipe(1)] replaces a missing parameter with 1, then [ParseIntPipe] converts it;
  • lines 30–33: [@Query()], without any arguments, injects an object containing all the parameters from URL.

The results:

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/parameters/action01?name=martin"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 31

name = [martin], of type string

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/parameters/action01"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 37

name = [undefined], of type undefined

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/parameters/action02?age=42"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 26

age = [42], of type string

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/parameters/action03?age=42"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 26

age = [42], of type number

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/parameters/action03?age=abc"

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 99

{"message":"Validation failed (numeric string is expected)","error":"Bad Request","statusCode":400}

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/parameters/action04"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 26

page = [1], of type number

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/parameters/action04?page=2"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 26

page = [2], of type number

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/parameters/action05?name=martin&age=42"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 28

{"name":"martin","age":"42"}

The quotation marks around URL are necessary when it contains the character [&], which has a specific meaning for the console. Note that:

  • a missing parameter is treated as [undefined];
  • a present parameter is a string, regardless of the declared type;
  • a pipe is used to convert and validate a parameter, and returns a 400 status code if the value is invalid.

docs.title: 3.2. Example 08: An action template described by a class
docs.text:
When an action has multiple parameters, they are described by a class, often called [DTO] ([Data Transfer Object]). Each field of the class has validation decorators provided by the [class-validator] library. These are equivalent to the attributes [[Required]], [[Range]]..., etc., of [ASP.NET MVC].

The [src/person.dto.ts] file:

import { Type } from 'class-transformer';
import { IsEmail, IsIn, IsInt, IsNotEmpty, IsOptional, Length, Max, Min } from 'class-validator';

export class PersonDto {
  @IsNotEmpty({ message: 'the name is required' })
  @Length(2, 20, { message: 'the name must have 2 to 20 characters' })
  name: string;

  @Type(() => Number)
  @IsInt({ message: 'the age must be an integer' })
  @Min(0, { message: 'the age must be positive' })
  @Max(150, { message: 'the age cannot exceed 150' })
  age: number;

  @IsIn(['Mr', 'Mme', 'Melle'], { message: 'unknown title' })
  title: string;

  @IsOptional()
  @IsEmail({}, { message: 'invalid email address' })
  email?: string;
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 1: [@Type] comes from the [class-transformer] library, which converts the received data;
  • line 2: the validation decorators from [class-validator];
  • lines 5–7: the name is required ([@IsNotEmpty]) and must be between 2 and 20 characters long ([@Length]). Each decorator accepts a custom error message;
  • lines 9–13: [@Type(() => Number)] requires the received string to be converted to a number before validation: an integer ([@IsInt]) between 0 and 150 ([@Min], [@Max]);
  • lines 15–16: the title must be one of the values in a list;
  • lines 18–20: the email address is optional ([@IsOptional]); if present, it must be valid ([@IsEmail]).

The file [src/persons.controller.ts]:

import { Controller, Get, Query } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PersonDto } from './person.dto';

@Controller('persons')
export class PersonsController {
  // /persons/action01?name=martin&age=42&title=Mr
  @Get('action01')
  action01(@Query() person: PersonDto): object {
    return {
      person,
      ageType: typeof person.age,
      isAPersonDto: person instanceof PersonDto,
    };
  }
}

line 8: the action receives a [PersonDto]. The action returns the received person, their age type, and verifies that it is indeed an instance of the [PersonDto] class.

To ensure that the class’s decorators are applied, validation must be enabled once and for all in [main.ts]:

The file [src/main.ts]:

import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  // automatic validation of ALL action models described by a class
  app.useGlobalPipes(
    new ValidationPipe({
      transform: true, // converts the received strings to the declared types
      whitelist: true, // removes the fields not declared in the class
    }),
  );
  await app.listen(3000);
  console.log('Server started on http://localhost:3000');
}

bootstrap();
  • lines 8–13: A global pipe, [ValidationPipe], is applied to all parameters of all actions. For a parameter whose type is a class, it checks the constraints of its decorators;
  • line 10: [transform: true]: the action receives a true instance of [PersonDto], whose fields have been converted ([@Type]);
  • line 11: [whitelist: true]: Parameters that do not correspond to any field in the class are removed.

A valid request with a parameter ([pirate]) that is not declared in the class:

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/persons/action01?name=martin&age=42&title=Mr&pirate=1"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 89

{"person":{"name":"martin","age":42,"title":"Mr"},"ageType":"number","isAPersonDto":true}

The age has indeed become a number, and the parameter [pirate] has disappeared. An invalid query:

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/persons/action01?name=m&age=abc&title=Dr&email=xx"

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 216

{"message":["the name must have 2 to 20 characters","the age cannot exceed 150","the age must be positive","the age must be an integer","unknown title","invalid email address"],"error":"Bad Request","statusCode":400}

[ValidationPipe] rejected the request with a 400 error, the body of which (JSON) lists the error messages. The action was not executed. The same result occurs without any parameters:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/persons/action01

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 215

{"message":["the name must have 2 to 20 characters","the name is required","the age cannot exceed 150","the age must be positive","the age must be an integer","unknown title"],"error":"Bad Request","statusCode":400}

This behavior is expected for a JSON server, queried by a [JavaScript] client that displays errors in its own way. For a HTML application, an error JSON makes no sense: we want to redisplay the form with its errors. The following example shows how to take control.

docs.title: 3.3. Example 09: Validation Performed by the Action
docs.text:
Example 09 does not have a global [ValidationPipe]. The action itself converts and validates the model, using the same decorators (the [person.dto.ts] file is identical):

The [src/persons.controller.ts] file:

import { Controller, Get, Query } from '@nestjs/common';
import { plainToInstance } from 'class-transformer';
import { validate } from 'class-validator';
import { PersonDto } from './person.dto';

@Controller('persons')
export class PersonsController {
  // no ValidationPipe here: the action receives the RAW parameters and
  // decides itself what to do with the errors
  @Get('action01')
  async action01(@Query() raw: Record<string, string>): Promise<string> {
    // 1. raw object -> PersonDto instance (@Type conversions included)
    const person = plainToInstance(PersonDto, raw);
    // 2. checking the constraints (@IsNotEmpty, @Min...)
    const errors = await validate(person);
    // 3. an HTML page in both cases: no 400 error
    if (errors.length === 0) {
      return `<p>Welcome ${person.title} ${person.name} (${person.age} years old)</p>`;
    }
    const items = errors
      .map((e) => `<li>${e.property}: ${Object.values(e.constraints ?? {}).join(', ')}</li>`)
      .join('');
    return `<p>The form contains errors:</p><ul>${items}</ul>`;
  }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 11: the action receives the raw parameters: an object whose fields are all strings;
  • line 13: [plainToInstance] ([class-transformer]) creates an instance of [PersonDto] from the raw object, applying the conversions ([@Type]);
  • line 15: [validate] ([class-validator]) checks all constraints. It returns an error array, which is empty if everything is OK. Each error indicates the problematic field ([property]) and the messages for the violated constraints ([constraints]);
  • lines 17–18: no errors—a welcome page;
  • lines 20–23: otherwise, a page listing the errors. In both cases, the response is a HTML page, with status code 200.

This is the technique that all forms in the case study will use (see Example 19).

docs.title: 3.4. Example 10: Multiple Parameters
docs.text:
A single parameter can appear multiple times in a request: this is the case with checkboxes on a form or a multiple-selection list ([?color=red&color=green]).

The file [src/arrays.controller.ts]:

import { Controller, Get, Query } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ChoiceDto } from './choice.dto';

@Controller('arrays')
export class ArraysController {
  // /arrays/action01?color=red&color=green: what Express receives
  @Get('action01')
  action01(@Query('color') color: string | string[]): object {
    return { color, isAnArray: Array.isArray(color) };
  }

  // /arrays/action02?color=red: always an array thanks to ChoiceDto
  @Get('action02')
  action02(@Query() choice: ChoiceDto): object {
    return { colors: choice.color, count: choice.color.length };
  }
}

The [action01] action (lines 7–10) shows what an action receives:

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/arrays/action01?color=red"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 33

{"color":"red","isAnArray":false}

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/arrays/action01?color=red&color=green"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 42

{"color":["red","green"],"isAnArray":true}

The type depends on the number of values: a string for a single value, an array for multiple values. This is a common pitfall. The [ChoiceDto] class handles both cases as an array:

The file [src/choice.dto.ts]:

import { Transform } from 'class-transformer';
import { ArrayMinSize, IsArray, IsIn } from 'class-validator';

export class ChoiceDto {
  // ?color=red -> "red"; ?color=red&color=green -> ["red","green"]
  // @Transform turns both cases into an array
  @Transform(({ value }) => (Array.isArray(value) ? value : [value]))
  @IsArray()
  @ArrayMinSize(1, { message: 'choose at least one color' })
  @IsIn(['red', 'green', 'blue'], { each: true, message: 'unknown color' })
  color: string[];
}
  • line 7: [@Transform] ([class-transformer]) applies a conversion function to the field: a single value is placed in an array;
  • line 8: the field must be an array...
  • line 9: ...with at least one element...
  • line 10: ... and each element ([each: true]) must be in the list.
curl -i "http://localhost:3000/arrays/action02?color=red"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 28

{"colors":["red"],"count":1}

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/arrays/action02?color=red&color=green"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 36

{"colors":["red","green"],"count":2}

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/arrays/action02?color=red&color=black"

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 68

{"message":["unknown color"],"error":"Bad Request","statusCode":400}

docs.title: 3.5. Example 11: Parameters of a POST request
docs.text:
A HTML form sent using the POST method places its fields in the request body, not in the URL. The [@Body] decorator then replaces [@Query]:

The file [src/post.controller.ts]:

import { Body, Controller, Headers, Post } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PersonDto } from './person.dto';

@Controller('post')
export class PostController {
  // the request body, as is
  @Post('action01')
  action01(@Body() body: Record<string, unknown>, @Headers('content-type') type: string): object {
    return { receivedType: type, body };
  }

  // a single field of the body
  @Post('action02')
  action02(@Body('name') name: string): string {
    return `name = [${name}]`;
  }

  // the body, converted and validated by the PersonDto class
  @Post('action03')
  action03(@Body() person: PersonDto): object {
    return { person, ageType: typeof person.age };
  }
}
  • lines 7–10: [@Body()] inserts the request body, which has already been decoded by [NestJS]. [@Headers('content-type')] inserts a request header: the body type;
  • lines 13–16: [@Body('name')] inserts a single field from the body;
  • lines 19–22: as with [@Query], the body can be described by a class, validated by the global [ValidationPipe].

The [-d] option of [curl] sends a POST request with a body in the format of a HTML form ([application/x-www-form-urlencoded]):

curl -i -d "name=martin&age=42" http://localhost:3000/post/action01

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 88

{"receivedType":"application/x-www-form-urlencoded","body":{"name":"martin","age":"42"}}

The same body in JSON format (this is what a client sends in [JavaScript] format):

curl -i -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"name":"martin","age":42}' http://localhost:3000/post/action01

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 69

{"receivedType":"application/json","body":{"name":"martin","age":42}}

[NestJS] decodes both formats. Note that “age” is a string in the first case (a HTML form carries only text) and a number in the second. The other two actions:

curl -i -d "name=martin&age=42" http://localhost:3000/post/action02

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 15

name = [martin]

curl -i -d "name=martin&age=42&title=Mme" http://localhost:3000/post/action03

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 70

{"person":{"name":"martin","age":42,"title":"Mme"},"ageType":"number"}

curl -i -d "name=martin&age=200" http://localhost:3000/post/action03

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 96

{"message":["the age cannot exceed 150","unknown title"],"error":"Bad Request","statusCode":400}

Code 201 (Created) is the default code for a POST for [NestJS]. For a HTML application, a POST action responds either with a page (in which case [@HttpCode(200)] is added) or with a redirect (see Example 20).

docs.title: 3.6. Example 12: Custom pipes and decorators
docs.text: You can write your own pipes and parameter decorators. The case study makes moderate use of them, but understanding them helps in understanding those of [NestJS].

docs.title: 3.6.1. A pipe: DateFrPipe
docs.text:
The file [src/date-fr.pipe.ts]:

import { BadRequestException, Injectable, PipeTransform } from '@nestjs/common';

// turns a French date "23/09/2026" into an ISO date "2026-09-23"
@Injectable()
export class DateFrPipe implements PipeTransform<string, string> {
  transform(value: string): string {
    const m = /^(\d{2})\/(\d{2})\/(\d{4})$/.exec(value ?? '');
    if (!m) {
      throw new BadRequestException(`[${value}] is not a date in the dd/mm/yyyy format`);
    }
    const [, day, month, year] = m;
    const iso = `${year}-${month}-${day}`;
    // "31/02/2026" has the right shape, but does not exist
    if (new Date(`${iso}T00:00:00Z`).toISOString().slice(0, 10) !== iso) {
      throw new BadRequestException(`the date [${value}] does not exist`);
    }
    return iso;
  }
}
  • lines 4–5: a pipe is a class [@Injectable()] that implements the interface [PipeTransform<input, output>];
  • line 6: its method [transform] receives the parameter value and returns the transformed value, which will be received by the action;
  • lines 7–9: a value that does not have the form [dd/mm/yyyy] triggers a [BadRequestException] (400);
  • lines 13–15: a date that is in the correct format but does not exist (31/02/2026) is also rejected: [new Date] “corrects” it to 03/03/2026, which is detected.

docs.title: 3.6.2. A parameter decorator: @Language()
docs.text:
The file [src/language.decorator.ts]:

import { createParamDecorator, ExecutionContext } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Request } from 'express';

// @Language(): the browser's preferred language, read from the header
// "Accept-Language: fr-FR,fr;q=0.9,en;q=0.8" -> "fr"
export const Language = createParamDecorator((fallback: string | undefined, ctx: ExecutionContext): string => {
  const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest<Request>();
  const header = req.get('accept-language') ?? '';
  const first = header.split(',')[0].trim().slice(0, 2).toLowerCase();
  return first || fallback || 'fr';
});
  • Line 6: [createParamDecorator] creates a parameter decorator, similar to [@Query] or [@Body]. The function receives the decorator’s argument ([@Language('fr')]) and the query’s execution context;
  • line 7: the context provides access to the request [Express];
  • lines 8–10: the first two letters of the header [Accept-Language] are returned, which indicate the user’s preferred languages.

docs.title: 3.6.3. The controller
docs.text:
The file [src/examples.controller.ts]:

import { Controller, Get, Query } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DateFrPipe } from './date-fr.pipe';
import { Language } from './language.decorator';
import { SearchDto } from './search.dto';

@Controller('examples')
export class ExamplesController {
  // /examples/schedule?day=23/09/2026: a custom pipe
  @Get('schedule')
  schedule(@Query('day', DateFrPipe) day: string): string {
    return `schedule for the day [${day}]`;
  }

  // /examples/hello: a custom parameter decorator
  @Get('hello')
  hello(@Language('fr') language: string): string {
    return language === 'en' ? 'Hello!' : 'Bonjour !';
  }

  // /examples/search?keyword=nest&admin=true: [admin] is not declared
  @Get('search')
  search(@Query() search: SearchDto): object {
    return search;
  }
}
  • line 10: the pipe is used as [ParseIntPipe];
  • line 16: the decorator is used as [@Query];
  • Line 22: a template described by a class, this time using the [forbidNonWhitelisted] option from [ValidationPipe] (file [main.ts] below).

The [src/main.ts] file:

import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  app.useGlobalPipes(
    new ValidationPipe({
      transform: true,
      whitelist: true, // the undeclared fields are removed...
      forbidNonWhitelisted: true, // ... or, with this option, rejected (400)
    }),
  );
  await app.listen(3000);
  console.log('Server started on http://localhost:3000');
}

bootstrap();

Line 11: With [forbidNonWhitelisted: true], an undeclared parameter in the class is no longer silently suppressed; it causes a 400 error.

The results:

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/examples/schedule?day=23/09/2026"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Content-Length: 33

schedule for the day [2026-09-23]

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/examples/schedule?day=2026-09-23"

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 104

{"message":"[2026-09-23] is not a date in the dd/mm/yyyy format","error":"Bad Request","statusCode":400}

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/examples/schedule?day=31/02/2026"

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 89

{"message":"the date [31/02/2026] does not exist","error":"Bad Request","statusCode":400}

curl -i -H "Accept-Language: fr-FR,fr;q=0.9" http://localhost:3000/examples/hello

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 9

Bonjour !

curl -i -H "Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9" http://localhost:3000/examples/hello

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 6

Hello!

curl -i "http://localhost:3000/examples/search?keyword=nest"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 18

{"keyword":"nest"}

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
